Placenta xQTL Atlas Multi-ancestry regulatory genomics, fine-mapping, GWAS integration, cell-type attribution, and G×E Bhattacharya Lab About this atlas The Placenta xQTL Atlas integrates multi-ancestry molecular QTL mapping with cross-ancestry fine-mapping, GWAS colocalization, transcriptome-wide association analysis, cell-type attribution, genotype × pre-pregnancy BMI interaction analysis, and locus-level synthesis. The chapters present the analytical results and their biological interpretation as a single report. Each analysis layer is followed by focused literature context where applicable, and the final synthesis chapter prioritizes loci supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. Reading order The book is organized in four parts: regulatory architecture, GWAS integration, biological context, and integrated synthesis. The analytical report for each layer is followed by its literature context when a companion review is available.

1 Multi-ancestry placental xQTL analysis 1.1 Executive summary This report summarizes the multi-ancestry placental xQTL analysis: cohort-only genotype PCA on LD-pruned variants within each ancestry stratum, a conventional covariate set (first 5 genotype PCs + HCP factors + sex, maternal age, and cell-type fractions; maternal cell fraction excluded before correlation pruning at |r| > 0.9; HCP count optimized per ancestry × modality via module 25b; no covariate cap), a MAF ≥ 0.01 filter with a ≥ 5 minor-allele-count floor at the genotype intersection, Storey q-values (computed with the R qvalue package), and per-phenotype normalization of all modalities (TMM → variance-stabilizing transformation for the two count-based expression modalities; rank-based inverse-normal transformation for the ratio-based modalities; isoform usage mapped as within-gene relative-abundance ratios). Mapping covers 36 ancestry × modality × layer cells (EAS n ≈ 281, EUR n ≈ 136). The results narrative follows the figure progression of the developing-brain xQTL atlas (Wen et al., Science 2024): cohort landscape → calibration → the modality-wise regulation landscape → cross-ancestry regulation → the discovery catalog → functional characterization. Headline result: 8116 phenotype-level associations reach FDR ≤ 5% in the discovery layer (ungrouped scan for the 8 multi-phenotype modalities + the per-gene expression scan): 3606 in EAS and 4510 in EUR, implicating 1757 / 2243 unique genes respectively. This phenotype-level set is the input to cross-ancestry SuSHiE fine-mapping (Methods). At gene level, the combined cross-modality catalog contains 1404 EAS and 1654 EUR eGenes at FDR ≤ 5%, with per-modality grouped eGenes as the breakdown. Strongest association per ancestry: EAS: PGM1 (expression, grouped layer, q = 5.4e-29); EUR: ERAP1 (alt_polyA, ungrouped layer, q = 1.8e-35). Storey calibration estimates a signal fraction (π1) of 0–34% across cells. In high-signal cells Storey q-values are correspondingly more liberal than Benjamini–Hochberg (by up to the estimated π0); the per-cell comparison is in Calibration. The splicing modality splits by ancestry. At its modality-matched HCP count (HCP count optimization), EUR splicing yields 35 FDR ≤ 5% eGenes — under expression-derived covariates the layer carried no detectable signal, so the EUR splicing null was a covariate-specification artifact, now resolved. EAS splicing remains near-null in both the grouped (5 eGenes, best q = 0.0021) and ungrouped (5 phenotype-level hits) layers, its eGene yield is flat across the HCP grid, and its p-values depart only mildly from the null at the median (genomic-control λ = 1.51; Calibration). Three lines of evidence bear on the residual EAS null: The machinery detects splicing signal where it exists — the same pipeline and covariate machinery yield the EUR splicing catalog above at n ≈ 136, a higher detection floor (r² ≈ 0.19) than EAS (r² ≈ 0.10 at n = 281; Power analysis). A pure sample-power explanation is therefore insufficient for EAS: EUR splicing effects cleared a higher bar. The leading candidate is EAS-specific attenuation of the splicing phenotypes — EAS pools four cohorts spanning single- and paired-end protocols, and junction-level quantification is the most protocol-sensitive of the nine modalities. The EAS null is not a covariate artifact — eGene yield does not improve at any HCP count on the grid (HCP count optimization), and the mild median λ elevation with only a handful of FDR-significant hits is the signature of diffuse, individually weak effects rather than of residual confounding (which would inflate the median without bound) or of a dead layer (λ ≈ 1, no tail). The FDR-significant hits in the other modalities carry estimated r² of 0.00–3.59 — exactly the class of outsize effect the floor permits. Signal replicates across ancestries — cross-ancestry rank concordance of gene-level signal on the combined layer is Spearman ρ = 0.18 (top-100 overlap 31/100), with same-variant slope concordance 0.54 — the pattern expected of real, partially shared genetic regulation, not of artifact-driven signal. Carrier-count audit: clean. The MAC ≥ 5 floor (applied at the genotype intersection in module 23) propagated to every mapping output — minimum minor-allele carrier count across all tested pairs is 27 (EAS) and 13 (EUR). # Methods Adapted from the project methods document (methods_placenta_xqtl.docx). 1.1.1 Study cohorts and data Placental RNA-seq and genotype data were assembled from four cohorts (Table 1). NIEHS_RICHS contributed placenta RNA-seq and array genotypes under dbGaP controlled access. GUSTO contributed placenta RNA-seq and array genotypes through the study investigators. SNUH contributed placenta RNA-seq and genotypes available under SRA BioProject PRJNA820329 (102 RNA-seq runs). NIGMS contributed placenta RNA-seq and whole-exome sequencing (WXS) under SRA BioProject PRJNA671171 (154 RNA-seq runs and 95 WXS runs); each NIGMS subject was sampled at two placental sites, and the replicate libraries were averaged per individual before mapping. All genotype and transcriptomic data were processed against the GRCh38 no-alt analysis set (GCA_000001405.15). Study cohorts, data types, and access routes. 1.1.2 Genotype processing and imputation Array genotypes were lifted over to GRCh38 where required. For NIGMS, WXS reads were retrieved from SRA, aligned to GRCh38 with BWA, processed to per-sample gVCFs with GATK, and jointly genotyped per chromosome. Each cohort was filtered before imputation to biallelic SNPs with per-variant missingness of at most 0.05, minor allele frequency (MAF) of at least 0.01, and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) test P above 1 x 10^-6, and variants were left-aligned and normalized against the reference genome with bcftools norm. Genotypes were imputed on either the TOPMed (NIGMS, NIEHS_RICHS) or SEAD (GUSTO, SNUH) imputation servers. Imputed variants with imputation Rsq of at least 0.4 were retained and converted to plink2 binary format (pgen). 1.1.3 Ancestry assignment and cross-cohort genotype pooling Genetic ancestry was assigned within each cohort with PC-AiR as implemented in GENESIS, using kinship estimated with KING in SNPRelate and 1000 Genomes phase 3 samples as the unrelated reference set. Each sample was assigned to one of five continental ancestry strata (AFR, AMR, EAS, EUR, SAS). For each stratum, the Rsq-passing variants of each cohort were subset to the assigned samples, multiallelic sites were split per cohort so that imputed dosages were partitioned correctly, and cohort VCFs were merged across cohorts with bcftools merge and normalized against GRCh38. Pooled genotypes were filtered to MAF of at least 0.01, HWE P above 1 x 10^-6, and per-variant missingness of at most 0.05, and palindromic duplicate sites were removed. The resulting per-ancestry pgen files define the genotype identifier space used by all downstream steps. 1.1.4 RNA-seq processing RNA-seq reads for SNUH and NIGMS were retrieved from SRA with prefetch and fasterq-dump; GUSTO and NIEHS_RICHS FASTQs were already local. Adapters and low-quality bases were trimmed with Trim Galore 0.6.10. Reads were aligned to GRCh38 with STAR 2.7.4a in basic two-pass mode. Transcript abundance was quantified with Salmon 1.10.2 against the HPLRv2 long-read placental transcriptome annotation using automatic library-type detection, selective alignment with validateMappings, and 20 bootstrap replicates per sample. 1.1.5 Transcriptomic phenotyping Nine RNA modalities were quantified per sample with an in-house rewrite of the PANTRY phenotyping pipeline (github.com/PejLab/Pantry) adapted to the local compute cluster. Gene expression was quantified from Salmon with tximport, both as gene-level TPM (used for detection filtering) and as gene-level lengthScaledTPM count-scaled abundances (tximport countsFromAbundance = “lengthScaledTPM”), the latter serving as the TMM-VST normalization input. Isoform expression was taken as transcript-level TPM after quantification uncertainty correction (see below), with TPM recomputed from the QU-corrected counts and Salmon effective lengths; the QU-corrected transcript counts themselves served as the TMM-VST normalization input for isoform expression. Isoform usage was computed as within-gene relative abundance ratios after correcting transcript counts for quantification uncertainty: edgeR catchSalmon was used to estimate per-transcript overdispersion from the Salmon bootstrap replicates, and counts were divided by the estimated overdispersion (Chen et al., Nucleic Acids Res 2023). Alternative transcription start site and alternative polyadenylation usage were quantified with txrevise: event annotations were constructed in two event groups, each split into upstream, contained, and downstream positional classes, and event abundance was quantified with Salmon against the six resulting transcript indices. Splice junction usage was quantified by extracting junctions from the STAR alignments with RegTools and clustering them with leafCutter (minimum 30 reads per cluster, minimum cluster ratio 0.001); intron usage ratios within clusters were carried as phenotypes. Intron retention was quantified with MAJIQ. RNA editing levels were computed at REDIportal sites (TABLE1_hg38_v3) from samtools mpileup output as the proportion of edited reads per site. RNA stability was approximated per gene as the ratio of exonic to intronic read counts from featureCounts. Because splice junctions and retained introns are defined by the observed data in each cohort, splicing and intron retention features were harmonized across cohorts by stable genomic coordinates before pooling. Phenotypes were exported as bgzipped, tabix-indexed BED files with gene-level phenotype groupings where applicable. 1.1.6 Cell-type deconvolution Cell-type proportions were estimated from bulk gene expression with MuSiC, using a published placental single-cell RNA-seq reference (GSE182381). The estimated fractions were carried into the mapping covariates. 1.1.7 RNA to DNA sample linkage RNA-seq sample identifiers were linked to genotype sample identifiers within each cohort using cohort-specific keys: SRA run-to-subject metadata for SNUH and NIGMS, and array subject identifiers for NIEHS_RICHS and GUSTO. The linkage table was checked for match rates, duplicates, and missing values before mapping. 1.1.8 Phenotype pooling and normalization Within each ancestry stratum, per-cohort phenotype matrices were pooled and normalized in a single pass. The two count-based expression modalities (gene expression and isoform expression) followed the PsychENCODE/isoTWAS convention (Bhattacharya et al., Nat Genet 2023): after the detection filter, pooled count matrices — gene-level lengthScaledTPM counts from tximport for gene expression, and QU-corrected transcript counts for isoform expression — were normalized with edgeR TMM followed by the DESeq2 variance-stabilizing transformation, with TMM effective library sizes supplied to DESeq2 as size factors (counts themselves never pre-divided), and no subsequent rank transformation. The six ratio-based modalities followed the conventions of the developing-brain xQTL atlas (Wen et al., Science 2024): filtered matrices were quantile normalized across the pooled stratum, and each phenotype was then rank inverse-normal transformed separately within each cohort, so every cohort enters mapping on an identical standard-normal scale. Gene and isoform expression were filtered to features with TPM above 0.1 in more than 25% of samples (the filter is computed on the TPM matrices and the retained feature set is carried onto the count matrices), and ratio-based modalities were filtered to features detected in at least 40% of samples. For expression, sample outliers were removed from the normalized matrix using signed bicor network connectivity (z below -3). Cohort effects are absorbed by cohort indicator covariates in the mapping model — and, for the VST-normalized expression modalities, by cohort indicators included as known covariates during hidden-factor estimation — rather than by adjusting the phenotype matrix. 1.1.9 Genotype principal components and sample quality control Within each stratum, pooled genotypes were LD-pruned (plink2 indep-pairwise 200 50 0.2) and 20 principal components (PCs) were computed exactly; the first five PCs were retained as covariates. Genotype and phenotype sample sets were intersected on the linkage map, and variants were further required to have a minor allele count of at least 5 in the intersected samples. Samples more than 6 standard deviations from the mean on any of the first five genotype PCs were excluded. 1.1.10 Covariate assembly and hidden factor estimation Mapping covariates comprised the first five genotype PCs, sex, maternal age, estimated cell-type fractions (with the dominant cell type as the compositional reference and the maternal fraction excluded), cohort indicator covariates, and hidden confounding factors estimated from the normalized expression matrix with Rhcpp, using Picard alignment quality-control metrics and cohort indicators as known covariates. Covariates with near-zero variance were dropped, and the remaining set was pruned iteratively at pairwise absolute correlation above 0.9, with retention priority given to sex and maternal age, then genotype PCs, then cell types, then hidden factors. The number of hidden factors was optimized separately for each ancestry and modality: factors were re-estimated at each k in {0…5…100} by 5, chromosome 1 was mapped with tensorQTL under each candidate covariate set (the full genome was mapped for modalities with fewer than 300 chromosome-1 phenotypes), and the k yielding the most eGenes at Storey q of at most 0.05 was selected, with ties resolved to the smaller k. 1.1.11 cis-xQTL mapping cis-QTL mapping was performed per ancestry stratum and modality with tensorQTL 1.0.10 under GTEx conventions: a cis window of 1 Mb on either side of the phenotype start, MAF of at least 0.01, nominal and permutation passes, and Storey q-values computed on the permutation beta-approximated P values with the R qvalue package. For modalities with gene-level phenotype groupings, grouped permutation (group_s) was used to select one lead variant per gene; the remaining modalities were mapped ungrouped. Multiple independent signals per gene (grouped layers) or per phenotype (ungrouped layer) were identified with the stepwise conditional mode (map_independent). Three result layers were produced per ancestry: grouped, ungrouped, and a combined cross-modality layer in which phenotype identifiers are namespaced by modality. 1.1.12 Cross-ancestry fine-mapping FDR-significant lead phenotypes (q of at most 0.05) were pooled across ancestries per modality — from the primary per-gene scan for expression and from the ungrouped phenotype-level scan for all other modalities — and each locus was fine-mapped jointly across ancestries with SuSHiE (version 0.20 or later) in individual-level mode, using in-sample linkage disequilibrium from the intersected genotypes and the exact tested cis windows. The number of effects per locus was set to min(10, max(5, n_independent + 2)), where n_independent is the number of stepwise-conditional signals at the locus, and credible sets were filtered at a purity threshold of 0.5. Per-variant posterior inclusion probabilities (PIPs), credible-set membership, per-ancestry effect weights, and the cross-ancestry effect-size correlation were recorded for each locus. 1.1.13 Functional enrichment of fine-mapped variants High-confidence variants (PIP of at least 0.9) were compared against all fine-mapped variants for enrichment in functional annotations. Variant consequences were annotated with fastVEP (GRCh38) and grouped into splice, loss-of-function, missense, synonymous, UTR, intron, regulatory, flanking, and intergenic classes. Regulatory annotations comprised ENCODE SCREEN candidate cis-regulatory element classes and placenta open-chromatin regions. Enrichment was tested with Fisher exact tests as the primary analysis, logistic regression adjusting for log10 distance to the transcription start site as a sensitivity analysis, and PIP-weighted enrichment; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR was applied within each test family. 1.1.14 Report-integration targeted lookups To support cross-ancestry and cross-modality report panels without shipping genome-wide summary statistics, targeted association lookups were performed (script 35): for each FDR-significant lead (variant, phenotype) pair, the same pair’s slope, standard error, and nominal P value were recomputed in the other ancestry stratum and, for grouped-layer leads, across the gene’s phenotypes in every other modality within the same ancestry, by ordinary least squares on covariate-residualized genotypes and phenotypes. All unique lead variants were annotated with fastVEP consequence classes and intersected with ENCODE cCRE classes and placenta open-chromatin regions, and per-gene loss-of-function constraint metrics (pLI, LOEUF) were taken from gnomAD v2.1.1. Regional association scans (plus-minus 1 Mb) with linkage disequilibrium (r^2) to the lead variant were computed for two showcase loci (ERAP2 and the top shared non-expression-driver locus). 1.1.15 Software and computing All pipeline stages were run on the MD Anderson seadragon high-performance computing cluster (LSF scheduler, RHEL8). S3/S5/S6 (per-modality mapping QC: HCP optimization, permutation calibration, signal fraction). 1.2.1 Pipeline recap Phenotypes: 9 RNA modalities (gene expression, isoform usage, isoform expression, splice junction usage, intron retention, alternative TSS, alternative polyA, RNA editing, RNA stability), harmonized to genotyped samples (array_id), with NIGMS technical replicates averaged per individual. The two isoform modalities are both built from QU-corrected Salmon transcript counts (mean count ≥ 10), length-normalized to TPM (count / effective length, scaled per sample to sum to 10^6): isoform usage is within-gene relative-abundance ratios (transcript TPM / gene-total TPM; PANTRY convention, mean ratio in \[0.05, 0.95\]) and isoform expression is the pre-ratio transcript TPM abundance (DevBrain §3.3 convention). Per ancestry stratum: feature filtering (isoform usage: usage > 0.1 in > 25% of samples; isoform expression: TPM > 0.1 in > 25% of samples, DevBrain §3.3; ratio modalities: detected in ≥ 40%, DevBrain §3.4). The two count-based expression modalities (gene expression, isoform expression) are then normalized by edgeR TMM -> DESeq2 VST on the pooled count matrices (gene-level lengthScaledTPM counts; QU-corrected transcript counts), terminal — no rank-based INT — with cohort indicators as known covariates in HCP estimation and in the mapping model (PsychENCODE/isoTWAS convention). The ratio-based modalities are batch-median NA-imputed, quantile-normalized across the pooled stratum + rank-based inverse-normal transformed per phenotype within each cohort, with cohort indicator covariates in the mapping model absorbing residual cohort effects. For the INT modalities no log2 pre-transform is applied: rank-based INT is invariant to any monotone transform, so log2/VST would be exact no-ops on the mapped scale. Genotypes: ancestry-stratified plink2 pgen; variants filtered to MAF ≥ 0.01 with MAC ≥ 5 (≥ 5 minor alleles) at the genotype intersection — the count floor excludes low-carrier tests, which can produce spurious associations, while MAF 0.01 keeps the variant pool as large as defensible. tensorQTL’s own MAF ≥ 0.01 filter applies on top at mapping time. Genotype PCA: cohort-only PCA per ancestry on LD-pruned variants (plink2 --indep-pairwise 200 50 0.2, then --pca 20 exact) — the GTEx convention. Covariates: per ancestry × modality, first-5 genotype PCs + HCP factors 1–k* (k* selected per ancestry × modality by module 25b, chr1 eGene maximization on each modality’s own HCPs) + sex + maternal age + cell-type fractions (Syncytiotrophoblast as reference). The maternal cell-fraction covariate (ct_Maternal) is excluded BEFORE pruning by analysis decision (coded --exclude-covariates); the remaining pool is correlation-pruned (iterative max-|r| > 0.9 removal, protecting sex > PCs > cell types > HCPs — correlated HCPs are dropped, so effective k can fall below nominal k*) with no covariate cap (details and QC below). Mapping (tensorQTL, cis window ±1 Mb): (i) per-modality grouped — all phenotypes of a gene within a modality tested as one group (permutation-calibrated gene-level p-value; the row label is the driver phenotype); (ii) combined — all phenotypes of a gene across all modalities as one cross-modality group (PANTRY’s headline design); \(iii\) ungrouped — per-phenotype lead variants for transcript-level resolution, and the discovery layer of record for fine-mapping; \(iv\) stepwise (cis.map_independent) for conditionally independent signals, entered at FDR ≤ 5% and run on the grouped, ungrouped, and combined layers alike. Multiple testing: Storey q-values on the permutation-calibrated p-value (pval_beta), computed with the R qvalue package (default lambda) — the GTEx convention, and statistically identical to tensorQTL’s own calculate_qvalues. (On this cluster the rpy2/conda-R route to qvalue hits an unresolvable libstdc++/GLIBCXX conflict, so q-values are computed through a file-based bridge to the singularity R container used elsewhere in the pipeline.) 1.2.2 HCP count optimization (module 25b) 1.2.3 Permutation-calibrated p-value QQ plots Two reference points calibrate the reading. enrichment caches with a reproducible analysis built from the same archive used by the rest of this report. On the first render for an archive — or whenever the archive’s ungrouped top scan tables, gene_map.tsv, or the static pregnancy-set annotation are newer than the cached enrichment output — the report rebuilds the per-modality ORA locally. The derived enrichment files are written under the archive-specific subdirectory of params$derived_dir; they are never read from inputs_freeze/xqtl_enrichment_report_files. Two complementary analyses are shown: Per-modality ORA — genes carrying at least one significant cis-xQTL (q < 0.05) in the ungrouped top-variant scan, separately for 8 multi-phenotype modalities x 2 ancestries. GO BP/MF/CC, KEGG, MSigDB Hallmark, and a curated pregnancy/placenta collection are tested under two universes: the HPLRv2 reference annotation and the genes tested in the corresponding ancestry-modality stratum. Combined-catalog ORA — combined-layer eGene sets (per ancestry, shared, and ancestry-specific) are queried with g:Profiler against the matching tested-gene background. This remains an optional live-service analysis and is skipped cleanly when g:Profiler is unavailable. 1.6.1 Per-modality enrichment of xQTL gene sets modality ancestry tested_genes sig_genes sig_novel_HPLRG isoform_expression EAS 12309 993 7 isoform_expression EUR 13081 1241 25 isoforms EAS 9049 263 0 isoforms EUR 9221 175 3 splicing EAS 5252 5 0 splicing EUR 7577 23 0 intron_retention EAS 1800 54 0 intron_retention EUR 2591 79 0 alt_TSS EAS 7715 95 0 alt_TSS EUR 7877 57 1 alt_polyA EAS 7273 176 0 alt_polyA EUR 7350 222 0 RNA_editing EAS 353 20 0 RNA_editing EUR 882 82 0 stability EAS 4492 140 0 stability EUR 7361 203 4 Per-modality discovery sets used for ORA The reference universe contains 13,835 HPLRv2 genes, including 533 HPLRG_ genes. When a large fraction of the tested universe is significant, only the strongest deviations from the background remain detectable; absence of enrichment does not imply absence of pathway biology. Annotation visibility is incomplete. HPLRv2-novel genes and Ensembl genes absent from a database’s identifier map can contribute to xQTL discovery but not to that database’s ORA. Pathway redundancy matters. Multiple significant terms can encode the same underlying gene cluster (especially HLA/immune and ribosomal terms), so term counts are not counts of independent biological mechanisms. Small curated sets have limited power. Pregnancy-set results should be interpreted from effect/overlap sizes as well as FDR. ORA is not causal. Enrichment can prioritize biology but cannot establish regulatory mediation of a pregnancy trait; colocalization and functional follow-up are required. Remote resources are snapshots. KEGG, MSigDB retrieval, and g:Profiler can change with database updates or be temporarily unavailable. The derived enrichment directory records the databases that were successfully built. Per-modality methods: input = ungrouped top-variant cis-QTL scan per modality x ancestry; significant genes = unique genes with q < 0.05 among tested features; universes = HPLRv2 PANTRY GTF genes or per-stratum tested genes; GO = clusterProfiler::enrichGO, KEGG = enrichKEGG after Ensembl-to-Entrez mapping, Hallmark/custom sets = enricher; BH FDR within each ancestry x modality x database x background; pregnancy sets use minGSSize = 3. Derived results are rebuilt from the current report archive. 1.7 Biological interpretation The discovery landscape: 8116 FDR ≤ 5% phenotype-level associations (3606 EAS / 4510 EUR, ungrouped + expression layers) implicating 1757 / 2243 unique genes, with the gene-level combined-layer catalog at 1404 EAS and 1654 EUR eGenes (n ≈ 281/136, MAF ≥ 0.01 + MAC ≥ 5, genome-wide permutation calibration). Strongest per ancestry: EAS: PGM1 (expression, grouped layer, q = 5.4e-29, r² ≈ 0.06); EUR: ERAP1 (alt_polyA, ungrouped layer, q = 1.8e-35, r² ≈ 0.59). Hit effect sizes (r² 0.00–3.59) sit in the class the power floor permits. All hits should be treated as candidates: visual QC of phenotype levels by genotype and replication in larger placental cohorts come before functional claims. Three characterization observations: Modality composition. expression leads the EAS grouped-eGene breakdown (1123 of 2889); expression leads the EUR grouped-eGene breakdown (1528 of 3627) PANTRY’s central finding was that non-expression modalities carry the largest share of regulatory signal; the driver-modality composition of the catalog (above) tests whether that ordering holds in placenta. Ancestry sharing. 572 of 1403 EAS and 1650 EUR combined-layer eGenes are shared (Fisher OR 6.44, p = 1.8e-173 vs the tested-in-both universe). Shared eGenes are the cross-ancestry replication signal; specific sets are candidates for ancestry-biased regulation. Functional enrichment. Top g:Profiler term per set: EAS combined eGenes — Metabolic pathways (KEGG, g:SCS p = 8.6e-08); EAS-specific eGenes — Metabolic pathways (KEGG, g:SCS p = 0.003); EUR combined eGenes — Glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism (KEGG, g:SCS p = 0.035); shared eGenes — Metabolic pathways (KEGG, g:SCS p = 0.0017). Full tables in tables/enrichment_*.tsv. 1.7.1 Literature context Modality-matched covariates, in line with QTL practice. Latent-factor covariates are a standard power lever in QTL mapping (Stegle et al. 2012), and splicing layers — quantified annotation-free from intron usage (Li et al. 2017) — have hidden structure that need not track gene expression. The per-modality HCP choice behaved as that practice predicts: EUR splicing was null under expression-derived factors and recovers 35 eGenes at its own modality-matched k*, while the EAS splicing null is flat across the entire k grid, excluding covariate specification as its cause. Sub-threshold top-ranked genes (tables above) remain prioritization hints only. 1.8 Limitations and next steps Power. n ≈ 281/136 with a ~12k-gene testing burden detects only r² ≳ 0.10 (EAS) / 0.19 (EUR) effects. Doubling n would roughly halve the detectable r²; matching PANTRY’s n = 445 would bring the floor to ≈ 0.06. Adding the remaining cohorts and the AFR/AMR/SAS strata is the highest-value next step. EAS splicing is near-null. The layer yields a handful of FDR ≤ 5% eGenes while EUR splicing — at a higher detection floor — yields 35. The EAS result is robust to HCP count (flat k-grid), so covariate specification is excluded as the cause; the leading candidate is cross-cohort heterogeneity in junction-level quantification (EAS pools four cohorts spanning single- and paired-end protocols). Revisiting splicing quantification harmonization across the EAS cohorts, and adding EAS cohorts, are the targeted next steps. Technical replicates. 25 mapped individuals (4 EAS, 21 EUR) have two RNA-seq runs. Phenotype values come from the single normalized run per individual, while run-level covariates (cell-type fractions, QC metrics) are averaged across the pair — a slight phenotype/covariate misalignment for those individuals. Future runs will collapse replicates at the count level before normalization so phenotypes and covariates are averaged consistently, with a pre-collapse replicate-concordance QC gate. Carrier-count propagation. The MAC ≥ 5 floor propagated cleanly to every mapping output (audit table above). Ancestry asymmetry. EUR tests more phenotypes than EAS in every modality (ancestry-specific filtering), so cross-ancestry comparisons are restricted to genes tested in both. No pooled cross-ancestry inference was performed. If combined discovery is wanted later, Fisher/Stouffer or an inverse-variance slope meta-analysis are the clean options. Stepwise secondary signals: 964 units carry a conditionally independent secondary signal (table above). Replication path: the FDR-significant hits are the priorities for lookup in larger placental resources or a future meta-analysis; visual QC of phenotype levels by genotype is the immediate sanity check for each. 1.9 Reproducibility Results: tensorQTL cis mapping (grouped / ungrouped / combined layers, each with stepwise cis.map_independent scans), MAF ≥ 0.01 + MAC ≥ 5 at the genotype intersection, ±1 Mb window, Storey q-values on pval_beta via the R qvalue package (singularity-R bridge). Covariates: as described (first-5 PCs + HCP_1–k* + sex/cell types; maternal fraction excluded before correlation pruning; no cap). Genotype PCs: cohort-only plink2 PCA on LD-pruned variants. Fine-mapping: SuSHiE joint cross-ancestry fine-mapping of the FDR-significant phenotype-level discovery set (ungrouped layer; expression from the primary scan), with fastVEP/cCRE/open-chromatin enrichment of high-PIP variants (scripts 31–34). Report extras: targeted cross-ancestry/cross-modality lookups, showcase locus scans, lead-variant annotations, and gnomAD constraint tables (05_qtl_mapping/35_extract_report_extras.py), staged into the archive under data/extras/ by make_report_archive.sh; report panels that use them render only when the corresponding file is present. 2 Literature context: placental xQTL mapping

2 Literature context: placental xQTL mapping Project: Placenta xQTL atlas (multi-ancestry, multi-modality cis-QTL mapping) Revision date: 2026-10-10 Companion analysis: report_placenta_xqtl.html Current result tables: tables/top_ungrouped_hits.tsv, tables/xqtl_catalog_phenotype_level.tsv, tables/phenotype_feature_counts.tsv, tables/egene_catalog_combined.tsv, and enrichment tables. Citation convention. Legacy bracketed citations [N] retain the indices from the original xqtl_top_hits_evidence_table.csv; their wording is preserved only where the corresponding gene remains in the current top-hit set. New literature or reference annotations added during this review are labeled [322]–[339] and are listed in the additional evidence (§9). This avoids renumbering the original evidence table. 2.0.1 1. Background and scope The atlas maps cis genetic regulation in placenta across gene expression plus eight multi-phenotype RNA-processing layers: isoform expression, isoform usage, splicing, intron retention, alternative transcription start sites (alt_TSS), alternative polyadenylation (alt_polyA), RNA editing, and transcript stability. The final mapped sample sets contain 281 EAS and 136 EUR individuals after genotype intersection, outlier removal, and technical-replicate collapse. The current mapping report contains 8,116 FDR-significant phenotype-level discovery associations (3,606 EAS and 4,510 EUR), implicating 1,757 EAS and 2,243 EUR unique genes across the discovery layer. At the combined gene-level layer there are 1,404 EAS and 1,654 EUR significant rows (1,403 and 1,650 unique gene IDs, respectively); 572 unique eGenes are shared across ancestries. This literature review focuses on the eight ungrouped multi-phenotype scans. For each modality and ancestry, the five lowest-q entries from the current top_ungrouped_hits.tsv are reviewed, yielding 80 top-table entries representing 56 unique gene symbols. A feature is labeled shared here when that same phenotype ID is present at q ≤ 0.05 in the opposite-ancestry phenotype-level catalog. By that definition, 39 of 80 top-table entries are shared. The purpose is descriptive rather than causal: to ask whether the strongest placental regulatory loci intersect known placental biology, prior QTL findings, or pregnancy-disease genetics, and to flag novel signals for mechanistic follow-up. 2.0.2 3. Methods Hit selection. Within each ancestry × ungrouped modality table, entries were ordered by Storey q-value and nominal p-value, and the top five were retained. Expression and the cross-modality combined scan are not part of this top-80 review because they do not have the same ungrouped multi-feature structure. Cross-ancestry sharing. “Shared” means the exact phenotype_id is FDR-significant (q ≤ 0.05) in both ancestries. Lead variants may differ. This is replication of a molecular feature, not proof of a shared causal variant and not a colocalization result. Atlas-wide counts. Significant-feature counts come from xqtl_catalog_phenotype_level.tsv; tested feature counts use the normalized (VST/INT) stage in phenotype_feature_counts.tsv. Literature synthesis. existing literature sources and numeric references were retained for genes still present. targeted literature searches were performed for newly entering genes, prioritizing PubMed papers with direct placental/pregnancy relevance, followed by mechanistic primary literature and curated reference resources when direct pregnancy literature was absent. Opposite-ancestry q-values. The supplied current tables include the significant catalog and top-10 tables, but not every non-significant ungrouped row. Therefore the tables report a binary shared flag rather than inventing or carrying forward stale q(other) values. 2.0.3 4. Overview of the current top hits Modality EAS sig./tested EUR sig./tested Shared among top 5×2 Isoform expression 1,333 / 37,217 1,603 / 41,150 8 / 10 Isoform usage 364 / 21,063 251 / 22,756 5 / 10 Splicing 5 / 56,258 28 / 79,006 0 / 10 Intron retention 56 / 3,818 102 / 10,765 0 / 10 Alternative TSS 184 / 29,868 90 / 37,279 5 / 10 Alternative polyA 371 / 26,322 459 / 33,027 10 / 10 RNA editing 30 / 3,120 246 / 17,951 7 / 10 Transcript stability 140 / 4,501 203 / 7,687 4 / 10 Alternative polyadenylation remains strikingly cross-ancestry reproducible at the top of the distribution (10/10). Isoform expression (8/10), RNA editing (7/10), isoform usage and alt-TSS (5/10 each) also contain substantial shared signal. By contrast, none of the selected splicing or intron-retention entries is shared at the exact-feature level. 2.0.3.1 4.1 Recurring multi-modality loci Several loci recur across independent molecular layers: ERAP1/ERAP2 (chr5q15). ERAP2 variant 5:96943786:A:G is the top EUR isoform-expression hit and drives two EUR promoter groups in opposite directions, including an HPLRv2 promoter. ERAP1 variant 5:96773906:G:A dominates both EUR isoform usage and alternative polyadenylation. This remains the atlas’s strongest convergence with established preeclampsia genetics. PSCA (chr8q24). Variant 8:142680513:C:T drives opposite effects on two PSCA isoforms and the corresponding polyA features; both polyA features and both isoform-usage features are cross-ancestry significant. ERGIC3 (chr20q13). Variant 20:35549038:C:T is a top EAS isoform-expression, intron-retention, and alt-TSS hit; the isoform-expression and alt-TSS features are shared across ancestries. MRPL43 (chr10q24). Variant 10:100963159:G:C is the top EAS intron-retention hit and a top EAS alt-polyA hit. PECAM1 (chr17q23). Variant 17:64322640:G:A appears in EUR isoform expression, isoform usage, and alternative polyadenylation, including an HPLRv2 polyA feature. GBP3 (chr1p22). Variant 1:89009135:A:G is a top EUR isoform-expression and transcript-stability signal, linking transcript abundance to post-transcriptional stability at an interferon-responsive locus. PSG9 (chr19q13). Variant 19:43303030:G:T is a top EAS intron-retention and stability signal in a placenta-specific pregnancy glycoprotein. MYL12B (chr18p11). Variant 18:3278477:A:G drives opposite effects on two EAS TSS groups, both shared across ancestries. HSP90B1 (chr12q23). Alternative-polyA features are strongly significant in both ancestries, with different lead variants in EAS and EUR. 2.0.3.2 4.2 Switch-like transcript regulation The clearest same-variant opposite-direction patterns are PSCA (isoform usage and polyA), ERAP1 (isoform usage and polyA), MYL12B (alt-TSS), ERAP2 (two EUR TSS groups), and SCARB2 (two EUR TSS groups). These loci are attractive for mechanism follow-up because the genetic effect appears to redistribute transcript identity or end choice rather than simply scale total RNA abundance. 2.0.3.3 4.3 Splicing: corrected interpretation after modality-matched HCP covariates In the current top five, EAS splicing lead AFs are approximately 0.053–0.098 and EUR lead minor-allele frequencies are approximately 0.052–0.054 (the TSR1 lead has AF 0.948, hence MAF ≈ 0.052). EUR top hits are concentrated around a chromosome-19 signal in which 19:44433568:C:T is the lead for ZNF234, APOC1P1/APOC1, and ZNF180. EAS remains a weak layer overall: only five ungrouped phenotypes reach FDR ≤ 5%. This is now best described as ancestry-asymmetric, modest-frequency splicing regulation, not as a set of extreme rare-variant associations. The concentration of several EUR rows under one lead and the shared CMYA5/TENT2 EAS splice cluster also reinforce the need for locus-level rather than naïve gene-by-gene interpretation. 2.0.3.4 4.4 HPLRv2-specific features among the top 80 Five current top entries explicitly carry HPLRT_* identifiers: TRIM5 and DRAM2 isoforms, an ERAP2 alt-TSS feature, an HSP90B1 alt-polyA feature, and a PECAM1 alt-polyA feature. These are concrete examples in which the long-read placental annotation exposes regulatory phenotypes absent from a standard transcript-only view. The chr22 ENSG00000290199 hit remains poorly characterized, but the current feature ID is ENST00000703580.1; therefore the statement that this transcript was necessarily “HPLRv2-only” has been removed. 2.0.3.5 4.5 RNA-editing coverage asymmetry The normalized RNA-editing feature universe is 17,951 in EUR versus 3,120 in EAS (~5.75×). Consequently, the 246 versus 30 significant editing phenotypes cannot be interpreted as a simple ancestry biology contrast. Shared sites such as CTNND1 and HSPD1 are particularly valuable because they replicate despite the strong coverage imbalance. 2.0.3.6 4.6 Atlas-wide ancestry sharing and functional context At the combined gene-level layer, 572 of 1,403 EAS and 1,650 EUR unique eGenes are shared. The current report estimates very strong enrichment for sharing relative to the tested-in-both universe (Fisher OR 6.44). Functional enrichment of combined and shared eGene sets is dominated by metabolic pathways, with “Metabolic pathways” the leading KEGG term for the EAS combined and shared sets. This broader metabolic signal complements—but should not be conflated with—the disease-focused literature enrichment apparent among the hand-selected top loci. 2.0.4 5. Modality-by-modality results and literature context 2.0.4.1 5.1 Isoform expression The strongest isoform-expression signals retain ERAP2/ZSCAN9 as positive controls but now bring RBM23 into the EAS top five and GBP3 into the EUR top five. Eight of the ten top-table entries correspond to features that are FDR-significant in both ancestries. Placental biology: phosphoglucomutase isozymes were purified from human placenta decades ago [199], but the gene’s modern literature is dominated by PGM1-CDG, a congenital glycosylation disorder treatable with galactose [200, 201]. No prior placental QTL or pregnancy-disease genetics — novel in this context. ERGIC3 (EAS2). Biology: an ER–Golgi intermediate compartment protein; the ERGIC is a stress-responsive hub integrating membrane trafficking and adaptation [155], and ERGIC3-dependent secretory cargo trafficking is regulated by the E3 ligase MARCH2 [156]. No placental literature — a novel, strongly shared, multi-modality locus. RBM23 (EAS3). Biology: RBM23 (CAPERβ) is a U2AF65-related RNA-binding protein that couples steroid-receptor transcriptional coactivation with alternative-splicing regulation [322]. I found no direct placental QTL or pregnancy-disease literature in the targeted literature search; the EAS isoform-expression QTL is therefore novel in placental context. ENSG00000290199 (EAS4). This chr22 locus is currently represented by Ensembl transcript ENST00000703580.1 and remains poorly characterized. The results support a large-effect EAS isoform-expression QTL that is also FDR-significant in EUR. The literature review called the feature “HPLRv2-novel”; because the current feature ID is an Ensembl transcript rather than an HPLRT identifier, that novelty claim has been removed. FBLN1 (EAS5). Placental biology: fibulin-1 is expressed during mouse placental development, with elevated transcripts in abnormal placentation [121]; in human pregnancy, plasma fibulin-1 rises across gestation and is consistently lower in PPROM [124]. No prior QTL evidence. ERAP2 (EUR1). Placental biology/disease: ERAP2 is one of the most replicated preeclampsia candidate genes: associated with preeclampsia in Australian and Norwegian cohorts [110], fetal ERAP2 rs2549782 associated with preeclampsia in African Americans [112], a Chilean haplotype study links rs2549782 to ERAP2 protein expression and PE risk [113], and ERAP1/ERAP2 show altered placental expression and lymphocyte activation in PE [107]; ERAP2 was also associated with PE (and ERAP1 with eclampsia) in Brazilian women [108]. Prior QTL evidence: ERAP2 was one of the notable eGenes in the Kikas et al. placental eQTL study [56] — the present hit is a direct cross-ancestry replication and extension to isoform- and promoter-level regulation. ZSCAN9 (EUR2). Prior QTL evidence: ZSCAN9 was likewise a notable placental eGene in Kikas et al. [56], making this a second direct replication. Biology: it is a KRAB zinc-finger protein; KRAB-ZFPs repress transposable elements and shape mammalian regulatory evolution [316, 317], a mechanism of particular relevance in placenta. The atlas continues to place multiple chromosome-19 zinc-finger loci among strong regulatory signals, although the specific top splicing genes have changed. GBP3 (EUR3). Biology: guanylate-binding proteins are interferon-induced pattern-recognition/antimicrobial effectors [114, 115]. Novel in placenta; joins OAS1 and TRIM5 in the innate-immunity theme. The same variant, 1:89009135:A:G, is also the EUR3 transcript-stability hit, making GBP3 a multi-modality innate-immune locus. PECAM1 (EUR4). Placental biology: CD31/PECAM-1 marks placental endothelium; microvessel density stained for CD31 is markedly reduced in preeclamptic placentas [222] and PECAM-1 expression is decreased in PE placentae [218], though one study found no difference in CD31 expression or vascular growth [223], and PECAM-1 itself does not appear to drive trophoblast invasion or PE/FGR pathophysiology [219]. The QTL is shared across ancestries and acts on both isoform abundance and polyA-site usage. SOHLH2 (EUR5). Biology: a germ-cell-specific bHLH transcription factor essential for oocyte and spermatogonial differentiation [202, 203, 204]. No prior placental QTL or pregnancy-disease association — a novel placental regulatory signal, plausibly reflecting its role in germline/early-lineage transcription programs. 2.0.4.2 5.2 Isoform usage The PSCA and ERAP1 switch-like loci remain dominant. The EUR fifth-ranked entry is now PECAM1, replacing ZNF880 from the literature review. A textbook isoform-switch QTL: the same allele lowers one PSCA isoform and raises the other. Literature: PSCA’s published record is entirely oncologic — expression rises with prostate cancer grade, stage, and metastasis [213], with context-dependent tumor-promoting or -suppressing roles [214] and prognostic/therapeutic interest across cancers [215]. There is no placental or pregnancy literature: this is a novel, cross-ancestry-shared placental isoform QTL for a GPI-anchored cell-surface antigen. OAS1 (EAS3). Placental biology: OAS1 is an innate immune sensor of dsRNA [95]; the placenta maintains baseline type I interferon/ISG signaling that preserves pregnancy homeostasis and antiviral readiness [97], and hemochorial placentas constitutively express type III interferon in trophoblasts [98]. A biologically coherent EAS-specific isoform QTL in the placental antiviral pathway. METTL2B (EAS4). Biology: an m3C tRNA methyltransferase with mutually exclusive substrate selection against METTL6 [283]; m3C32 modification controls serine codon-biased translation, cell cycle, and DNA-damage response [286]. Novel in placenta. PARP2 (EAS5). Disease relevance: PARP-family activity is mechanistically tied to placental dysfunction — NAD+ depletion from NAD+-consuming enzymes (including PARPs) marks an inflammatory subclass of preeclampsia and is reversible with nicotinamide riboside in models [271, 272], and PARP activation is elevated in gestational diabetic pregnancies [268]. Biology: PARP2 has distinct and shared functions with PARP1 in inflammation, metabolism, and oxidative stress [270]. ERAP1 (EUR1–2). An isoform-switch QTL mirroring PSCA. Disease: ERAP1 expression is elevated in preeclamptic placentas and inducible by hypoxia in trophoblasts [111]; ERAP1/ERAP2 placental expression and lymphocyte activation are altered in PE [107]; ERAP1 is associated with eclampsia in Brazilian women [108]. Prior QTL evidence: the adjacent ERAP2 was a notable placental eGene [56]; the present data resolve the locus into isoform- and polyA-level ERAP1 regulation. TRIM5 (EUR3). Biology: TRIM5α is a canonical retroviral restriction factor that recognizes and destabilizes incoming capsids [173], within the broader TRIM antiviral family [170]. No placental literature — novel; given the placenta’s constitutive antiviral state (see OAS1 below), a plausible innate-immunity locus. DRAM2 (EUR4). Biology: a lysosomal autophagy regulator; biallelic mutations cause retinal dystrophy [276], and despite divergence from DRAM it contributes to autophagy induction [277, 278]. Novel in placenta, where autophagy is central to trophoblast homeostasis. PECAM1 (EUR5). Placental biology: CD31/PECAM-1 marks placental endothelium; microvessel density stained for CD31 is markedly reduced in preeclamptic placentas [222] and PECAM-1 expression is decreased in PE placentae [218], though one study found no difference in CD31 expression or vascular growth [223], and PECAM-1 itself does not appear to drive trophoblast invasion or PE/FGR pathophysiology [219]. The QTL is shared across ancestries and acts on both isoform abundance and polyA-site usage. This same PECAM1 transcript is also among the top EUR isoform-expression hits, while a novel HPLRv2 polyA feature at PECAM1 is EUR4 in alt_polyA. 2.0.4.3 5.3 Splicing Under modality-matched HCP covariates, EUR splicing is no longer null and EAS is weak but nonzero. The old extreme 1% minor-allele-frequency LILRB/CNN2/DOCK8/SREK1/ZNF439/440 top set is not present in the results. Biology: ZFP62 is a poorly characterized human zinc-finger protein [333]. No direct placental or pregnancy literature was identified in the targeted literature search, so the EAS splicing association is currently best treated as an uncharacterized regulatory signal. CMYA5 (EAS2). Biology: CMYA5/myospryn is a very large striated-muscle protein induced by MEF2A, localized to the costamere, and interacting with α-actinin-2 [323]. Direct placental evidence is lacking; because the same splice cluster is also annotated to TENT2, gene attribution at this locus should remain cautious. CMYA5 and TENT2 are assigned to the same splice cluster and lead variant; gene attribution is therefore ambiguous. TENT2 (EAS3). Biology: TENT2/GLD2 is a non-canonical terminal nucleotidyl transferase involved in RNA 3′-end metabolism, a class of enzymes that regulates RNA stability and translation [324]. No direct placental disease evidence was found; the shared CMYA5/TENT2 splice-cluster annotation makes locus-level interpretation preferable to single-gene attribution. PLAC4 (EAS4). Placental biology/disease: PLAC4 is highly placenta-enriched, localizes to syncytiotrophoblast, increases with syncytialization, and was reported to be upregulated in severe early-onset preeclamptic placenta [325]. This makes the EAS PLAC4 splicing QTL one of the most directly placenta-relevant new hits created by the corrected splicing analysis. TRMT13 (EAS5). Biology: TRMT13 is a predicted tRNA methyltransferase involved in tRNA methylation [331]. Human Protein Atlas placental immunohistochemistry reports medium signal in decidual cells and low signal in trophoblastic cells [332]. No pregnancy-disease genetic literature was identified, so this is a new RNA-processing candidate rather than a known disease locus. ZNF234 (EUR1). Biology: ZNF234 is a chromosome-19 C2H2 zinc-finger protein predicted to regulate DNA-templated transcription [334]. Direct placental or pregnancy evidence was not identified. It participates in the same EUR chr19 splicing hotspot as APOC1/APOC1P1 and ZNF180. APOC1P1 (EUR2). Annotation: APOC1P1 is a transcribed/pseudogene locus adjacent to APOC1 [335]. Its top splice cluster is identical to the APOC1-annotated cluster, so the signal should be discussed as an APOC1/APOC1P1 locus rather than as independent evidence for the pseudogene. APOC1 (EUR3). Placental biology/disease: Recent placental single-cell/spatial multi-omics implicated APOC1 among central lipid-transport genes dysregulated in preeclampsia, with subtype- and cell-type-specific changes in EVT and Hofbauer cells [326]. A 2026 study further linked macrophage APOC1 deficiency to ferroptosis, inflammatory polarization, impaired trophoblast invasion, and recurrent pregnancy loss [327]. The EUR splicing signal therefore intersects a newly emerging maternal–fetal-interface literature. The APOC1 and APOC1P1 rows share the same splice cluster and lead variant, so these should not be read as independent mechanistic signals. ZNF180 (EUR4). Biology: ZNF180 is a Kruppel-related C2H2 zinc-finger protein with broadly expressed transcriptional-regulatory potential [336]. No direct placental disease literature was identified; its association shares the same EUR chr19 lead variant as ZNF234 and APOC1/APOC1P1. TSR1 (EUR5). Biology: TSR1 is a nucleolar RNA-binding ribosome-maturation factor implicated in pre-rRNA processing and small-subunit maturation [337]. No direct placental literature was identified, but the hit adds ribosome biogenesis to the RNA-processing signals represented among top xQTLs. 2.0.4.4 5.4 Intron retention The ancestry split remains strong: none of the ten top entries is FDR-significant in both ancestries. EAS is led by MRPL43/ERGIC3/PSG9; EUR by GM2A/IQGAP1/LGALS14/CYP19A1. The fifth EUR row is a second annotation of the CYP19A1 retention event. Synthesis 2.0.5.1 6.1 Agreement with prior placental QTL and pregnancy literature The strongest current loci continue to include direct placental-QTL positive controls. ERAP2 and ZSCAN9 were notable placental eGenes in the earlier Kikas et al. work [56], and the present atlas extends ERAP2 into transcript- and promoter-level regulation. SNX19 remains notable because genetically predicted placental expression has previously been associated with adult blood-pressure traits in a placental TWAS [194]. The disease-context signal is also robust to the hit list. Genes with substantial independent preeclampsia or maternal–fetal-interface evidence include ERAP1/ERAP2, HLA-C, LGALS14, CYP19A1, ANXA1, HSPD1, COX6C, PSG9, PECAM1, HSP90B1, and CTSB. The splicing layer adds PLAC4, a particularly compelling placenta-specific gene with direct severe early-onset preeclampsia and syncytialization evidence [325], and APOC1, which now has both preeclampsia multi-omics and recurrent-pregnancy-loss mechanistic support [A5, A6]. These overlaps are biologically coherent but should not be presented as disease colocalization. The atlas maps molecular traits in placenta; formal inference about mediation of pregnancy-disease GWAS requires the dedicated colocalization/TWAS analyses. 2.0.5.2 6.2 Recurring biological themes Immune regulation at the maternal–fetal interface: HLA-C, ERAP1/2, OAS1, TRIM5, GBP3, LGALS14, APOC1, and CTNND1. Placenta-specific/endocrine programs: PSG9, CYP19A1, PLAC4, and the galectin locus. Mitochondrial and cellular-stress biology: COX6C, MRPL43, HSPD1, HSP90B1, PARP2, APIP. Trophoblast structure, invasion, and membrane organization: IQGAP1, MYL12B, CTNND1, PECAM1, SCARB2, ERGIC3. RNA processing itself as a regulated phenotype: RBM23, TENT2, TRMT13, TSR1, RPL14, PPIE, the strong isoform/polyA switch loci. Lipid/immune-metabolic regulation: APOC1, PGAP6, SCARB2, GM2A, and the atlas-wide metabolic-pathway enrichment. 2.0.5.3 6.3 Novelty A substantial fraction of the 56 current top-hit genes still lack direct placental QTL or pregnancy-disease literature. The strongest “new biology” candidates include RBM23, ERGIC3, PSCA, TRIM5, DRAM2, ELP5, PGAP6, SCARB2, ENOSF1, ZFP62, ZNF234, ZNF180, TSR1, METTL2B, GM2A, VAMP8, SDR39U1, PPIE, SOHLH2, and the poorly characterized chr22 locus ENSG00000290199. Novelty here means that the targeted literature review did not identify direct prior placental/pregnancy evidence; it is not proof that no such paper exists. The five explicit HPLRv2 top features are additionally novel at the phenotype-definition level and demonstrate the value of the long-read reference. 2.0.5.4 6.4 A changed view of ancestry specificity The results separate three phenomena that were conflated previously: true feature-level replication, abundant for alt-polyA, isoform expression, and RNA editing; detection/phenotyping asymmetry, especially intron retention and RNA editing; covariate-specification sensitivity, dramatically illustrated by EUR splicing. Accordingly, absence of a shared top hit should not automatically be labeled an ancestry-specific biological effect. It can reflect phenotype observability, power, feature definition, or different LD/lead variants. The most defensible ancestry claims should come from matched-feature effect comparisons, cross-ancestry fine-mapping, and formal heterogeneity analyses. 2.0.6 7. Limitations Rank-selected review. Top five per ancestry/modality is a descriptive lens, not a genome-wide enrichment test and not a cross-ancestry meta-analysis. Shared does not mean same causal variant. The shared flag requires only FDR significance of the same molecular feature in both ancestries. Different lead variants can tag different causal configurations. Gene attribution can be ambiguous. This is especially important for the CMYA5/TENT2 splice cluster, APOC1P1/APOC1 cluster, CYP19A1 overlapping intron-retention annotations, and dense chromosome-19 zinc-finger regions. Splicing interpretation is covariate-sensitive. The corrected modality-matched HCP analysis resolves the prior EUR null, but EAS remains a low-yield layer and deserves cautious interpretation rather than overclaiming biological absence. Coverage differs by ancestry and modality. RNA editing is the clearest example (17,951 versus 3,120 normalized features). Effect estimates are discovery estimates. Large slopes, especially at lower-frequency variants, remain susceptible to winner’s curse. Abstract/reference-level literature review. The literature review was primarily abstract-level. New additions were also targeted rather than systematic. “No direct literature found” should be read literally as a search result, not as proof of novelty. No stale opposite-ancestry q-values. Exact q(other) values for non-significant features cannot be reconstructed from the attached top-10 and FDR-only tables; this review intentionally omits them. 2.0.7 8. Recommended follow-up from the literature review The strongest candidates for immediate integration with fine-mapping/colocalization are: ERAP1/ERAP2 (positive control and pregnancy genetics), PSCA (multi-layer switch), PECAM1 (endothelial and multi-layer), PSG9/LGALS14/PLAC4 (placenta-specialized biology), HLA-C/APOC1 (maternal–fetal immune interface), CTNND1/HSPD1 (cross-ancestry RNA-editing replication), and SCARB2/PGAP6/RBM23 as mechanistically interpretable but comparatively novel loci. For splicing specifically, follow-up should treat the chr19 19:44433568:C:T set as a single locus with multiple annotated consequences until conditional/fine-mapping evidence separates ZNF234, APOC1P1/APOC1, and ZNF180. 2.0.8 9. 4 Literature context: fine-mapped loci Project: Placenta xQTL atlas Revision: 2026-10-10, rebuilt against the newly supplied report_finemap.html, finemap_locus_summary.tsv, and finemap_credible_sets.tsv.gz. Companion literature review to report_finemap.html. It is the fine-mapping counterpart to literature_xqtl_mapping.md, which reviews the strongest variant-level association signals from the xQTL mapping report. 4.0.1 1. Background and scope The current fine-mapping run uses SuSHiE to resolve significant placental xQTL loci across nine molecular modalities: gene expression, isoform expression, isoform usage, splicing, intron retention, alternative transcription start sites, alternative polyadenylation, RNA editing, and transcript stability. The run report records 5,529 loci attempted, 5,269 successfully fine-mapped, and 4,290 loci with at least one credible set. this review does not retain the literature review’s claim of 5,236 high-confidence genes. Recalculation from the supplied results gives 2,055 current loci whose best credible set has lead PIP ≥ 0.9, spanning 1,142 unique Ensembl genes. Of those high-confidence loci, 1,899 (92.4%) have a single-variant credible set. Thus the strongest conclusion of the new run is not the sheer size of the gene catalog but the high degree of variant-level resolution among loci that pass the PIP threshold. The biological reading is also different from the literature review. The old fine-mapping review emphasized a splicing-heavy set of established pregnancy and imprinted genes. In the new run, many of those loci are absent or no longer reach PIP ≥ 0.9. Instead, the leading pattern is cross-modality recurrence: WSB1 is high-confidence in six modalities, while SCARB2 and OLAH are high-confidence in five. Established placental and pregnancy genes remain in the catalog — including CYP19A1, SIGLEC6, ERAP1, KISS1, LGALS14, PSG3, PSG9, PECAM1, and HSPD1 — but the conflict/imprinting lens is much smaller, with IGF2R and SGCE providing the clearest retained examples. Existing numeric citations [N] below preserve the numbering of the original fine-mapping literature review where the same literature-supported claim is retained. Newly added references are labeled [A1]–[A18] and are listed in Section 9. The companion finemap_hits_evidence_table.csv was not included with the new fine-mapping upload, so the new references are intentionally not assigned permanent numeric indices yet. 4.0.2 2. Methods and result reconciliation 4.0.2.1 2.1 Current-run membership The supplied finemap_credible_sets.tsv.gz contains 6,347 credible-set rows, matching the total displayed in the HTML report. However, 763 of those rows (534 phenotype IDs) do not occur in the newly supplied finemap_locus_summary.tsv. The 4,290 current loci with credible sets in the locus summary account for 5,584 credible sets. To prevent carry-over results from a previous mapping/fine-mapping run from entering the literature interpretation, all gene rankings in this review use only credible sets whose (modality, phenotype_id) pair is present in the new locus summary. This filtering step should also be incorporated into the report generation code, or the credible-set file should be regenerated cleanly. 4.0.2.2 2.2 High-confidence definition For each current (modality, phenotype_id) locus, the credible set with the highest lead_pip was selected. A locus is called high-confidence when that best credible set has lead_pip >= 0.9. Gene IDs were taken from the Ensembl prefix of phenotype_id. This gives: 2,055 high-confidence loci 1,142 unique genes 1,899 / 2,055 (92.4%) single-variant credible sets 405 genes high-confidence in at least two modalities 79 genes in at least three modalities 25 genes in at least four modalities only 3 genes in at least five modalities: WSB1, SCARB2, and OLAH. Cross-cutting patterns 4.0.3.1 3.1 Multi-modality recurrence replaces splicing dominance as the main signal The earlier review identified WSB1 and GBP3 as the most recurrent genes and then interpreted much of the pregnancy/conflict catalog through splicing. The new run retains WSB1 but changes the ranking substantially. WSB1 now spans six modalities, followed by SCARB2 and OLAH at five. Twenty-two additional genes span four modalities. The recurrent genes are therefore distributed across expression, isoform-level traits, RNA editing, RNA stability, and alternative ends rather than being dominated by one RNA-processing mechanism. WSB1 remains the clearest “genetics first, biology second” discovery. It has high-confidence signals in RNA editing, expression, intron retention, isoform expression, isoform usage, and stability. Its known biology — HIF-responsive ubiquitin regulation and functionally distinct splice isoforms [13,14] — makes the recurrence plausible in a hypoxia-responsive organ, but a direct placental role remains poorly characterized. SCARB2 and OLAH now join WSB1 as the two other five-modality genes. SCARB2 is a lysosomal membrane protein with strong protein expression in syncytiotrophoblast and Hofbauer cells [A1], while OLAH has unusually direct pregnancy relevance: placental OLAH changes across gestation and is altered in preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction; OLAH knockdown changes IGF2, oxidative-stress, and apoptosis-related transcription [A2]. 4.0.3.2 3.2 The high-confidence catalog is extremely well resolved A single-variant credible set is the minimum possible 95% CS. More than 92% of current PIP ≥0.9 loci are single-variant, and all 20 deep-dive genes have at least one such locus. This makes fine-mapping useful for variant prioritization, but the statistical precision should not be confused with mechanistic proof: a one-variant CS identifies a strong causal-regulatory candidate, not the molecular route by which it acts. 4.0.3.3 3.3 Established placental genes remain, but the positive controls changed The current high-confidence catalog still contains biologically reassuring placental genes, but not the exact set highlighted previously. CYP19A1, SIGLEC6, ERAP1, KISS1, LGALS14, PSG3, PSG9, PECAM1, HSPD1 and HSP90B1 all retain at least one single-variant PIP ≥0.9 signal. By contrast, FLT1, PAPPA, ACVR2A, HSD11B2, IGF2, PEG3, MEST and GNAS are not current high-confidence genes, and GCM1, HLA-C and MEG3 are present only below the 0.9 threshold. The implication is important: the literature review’s statement that fine-mapping “recovered known pregnancy genes as positive controls” was too dependent on an older result set. The new run should be interpreted from the loci it actually resolves, not from biologically attractive loci that were present previously. 4.0.3.4 3.4 Imprinting remains visible, but it is no longer a dominant catalog-wide theme The literature review highlighted six canonical imprinted genes and stated that 27 imprinted genes were present in the high-confidence set. That claim is not supported by the current files supplied here. Among the original six, only IGF2R remains PIP ≥0.9. A second clear current imprinted signal is SGCE, which has a single-variant isoform-expression credible set. SGCE is maternally imprinted [A17], is expressed across human gestation [A16], and together with IGF2R has been implicated in environmentally responsive placental imprinted-gene expression [A18]. Thus intragenomic conflict remains a useful biological lens, but it is now a focused secondary theme rather than one of the dominant statistical patterns. 4.0.4 4. Gene snapshots 4.0.4.1 4.1 Recurrent and placental-biology signals WSB1 — 6 modalities; 7 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. WSB1 is the most recurrent gene in the current fine-mapped catalog. The resolved modalities are RNA editing, expression, intron retention, isoform expression, isoform usage, and stability. WSB1 encodes the substrate-recognition component of an E3 ubiquitin ligase and participates in hypoxia signaling [13]. Its splice isoforms can have distinct effects on proliferation and apoptosis [14], making the breadth of RNA-level regulation biologically credible. Direct placental characterization remains limited, which keeps WSB1 among the atlas’s strongest novel candidates. SCARB2 — 5 modalities; 8 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. SCARB2/LIMP-2 is a lysosomal membrane receptor. Unlike WSB1, its placental presence is directly supported by tissue proteomics: SCARB2 is high in syncytiotrophoblast cell body and microvilli and in Hofbauer cells [A1]. Fine-mapping across RNA editing, alternative TSS, expression, isoform expression and isoform usage therefore nominates a lysosome/membrane-trafficking axis operating in both trophoblast and placental macrophage compartments. Mechanistic pregnancy literature is still sparse. OLAH — 5 modalities; 6 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. OLAH is the strongest newly validated pregnancy-relevant recurrent signal. A human placental study found that OLAH expression rises with gestation, is altered in preterm preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction, and responds to placental dysfunction; OLAH knockdown perturbed BAX, BCL2, IGF2 and NOX4 expression [A2]. The current fine-map spans RNA editing, alt-TSS, expression, isoform expression and stability, converting that disease-expression observation into a candidate genetically regulated placental pathway. CTSB — 4 modalities; 27 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. CTSB has the largest number of high-confidence loci among the selected genes, distributed across RNA editing, alt-polyA, expression and isoform expression. Cathepsin B protein is high in placental trophoblast [A3]; experimental trophoblast work places CTSB downstream of beta-catenin-dependent migration and invasion in a hypoxia/preeclampsia context [A4]. The striking number of resolved CTSB molecular phenotypes suggests that this locus is not a single expression QTL but a dense regulatory hotspot. GPNMB — 4 modalities; 12 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. GPNMB is resolved across alt-polyA, expression, isoform expression and isoform usage. Placental single-cell reference data show particularly strong expression in Hofbauer cells [A5], pointing to placental macrophages rather than trophoblast as the most likely cellular context. This is a useful example of why cell-type attribution should accompany bulk-placenta QTL interpretation. FOLR1 — 4 modalities; 5 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 0.99995; min CS = 1. FOLR1 encodes folate receptor-alpha, a core component of maternal-fetal folate transfer. FR-alpha localizes to the apical syncytiotrophoblast [A7], and placental FOLR1 expression/methylation has been studied in preterm birth [A6]. The four-modality fine-map — alt-TSS, expression, isoform expression and isoform usage — identifies several genetically controlled points at which placental folate transport could vary among individuals. GBP3 — 4 modalities; 7 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. GBP3 remains a recurrent innate-immunity signal, although its current recurrence is four rather than six modalities: expression, isoform expression, isoform usage and stability. GBPs are interferon-inducible antimicrobial GTPases [15], and GBP3 can participate in caspase-4-dependent pyroptosis [16]. There is still little direct placental literature, so GBP3 remains a high-confidence but biologically under-characterized maternal-fetal-interface candidate. HSP90B1 — 3 modalities; 4 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 0.99976; min CS = 1. HSP90B1/GRP94 is resolved at alternative polyadenylation, expression and isoform expression. Human Protein Atlas staining is high in both trophoblastic and decidual cells [A8]. The locus therefore adds genetically regulated endoplasmic-reticulum stress/chaperone biology to the same broad stress axis represented by HSPD1 below. 4.0.4.2 4.2 Pregnancy and trophoblast-function signals CYP19A1 — 3 modalities; 6 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. CYP19A1 remains a strong placental positive control, although the new run supports three modalities rather than five: alt-polyA, intron retention and isoform expression. Aromatase drives placental estrogen synthesis and has trophoblast-specific promoter biology [17]; placental CYP activity is altered in preeclampsia-related models [19]. Fine-mapping indicates that genetically regulated transcript architecture, not only total expression, is relevant at this canonical placental gene. SIGLEC6 — 2 modalities; 6 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. SIGLEC6 remains one of the most biologically specific placental hits. It is a placenta-enriched molecule and circulating biomarker candidate in preeclampsia [21], with mechanistic evidence connecting excess SIGLEC6 to impaired syncytialization and inflammatory polarization [22,23]. The current fine-map resolves RNA-editing and expression loci rather than the four modalities stated previously. ERAP1 — 4 modalities; 10 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. ERAP1 remains one of the most compelling pregnancy-disease loci in the catalog. It participates in MHC-I peptide processing and vasoactive peptide metabolism, has placental and preeclampsia evidence [28,29], and sits directly at the trophoblast-immune interface [30]. The current resolved modalities are RNA editing, intron retention, isoform expression and stability. This still supports unusually broad regulatory control, but the old expression/splicing claims should not be carried forward. IL1R1 — 3 modalities; 7 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 0.9986; min CS = 1. IL1R1 remains high-confidence across RNA editing, expression and isoform expression. IL-1 receptor signaling is a well-established inflammatory route into parturition and infection-induced preterm labor [43,44], and IL1R1 variation has been associated with chorioamnionitis risk [45]. The current fine-map therefore supports genetically regulated IL-1 responsiveness without requiring a splicing mechanism. KISS1 — 2 modalities; 2 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP ~1.00; min CS = 1. KISS1 is resolved for expression and isoform expression. Kisspeptin is tightly linked to trophoblast invasion: placental KISS1 is altered in preeclampsia, and experimental overexpression suppresses trophoblast invasion [A9,A10]. The QTL therefore provides a direct genetic route into a pathway already implicated in defective placentation. LGALS14 — 3 modalities; 4 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. LGALS14 is a primate placenta-associated galectin resolved for expression, isoform expression and stability. Galectin-14 promotes trophoblast migration and invasion and is reduced in early pregnancy loss and preeclampsia [A11]. The combination of placental specificity, disease dysregulation and single-variant QTL resolution makes LGALS14 a particularly interpretable fine-mapped locus. PSG3 — 3 modalities; 7 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. PSG3 is resolved for intron retention, isoform expression and isoform usage. Pregnancy-specific glycoproteins are produced in large amounts by placental trophoblast; PSG3 is among the genes strongly induced during trophoblast differentiation [A12]. The multi-layer signal suggests genetic control over both PSG3 abundance and transcript architecture. PSG9 — 2 modalities; 6 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. PSG9 is resolved for intron retention and isoform expression. Recent work identifies an LTR8B/PSG9 regulatory program controlling syncytialization and links elevated PSG9 to preeclampsia [A13]. The fine-mapped locus therefore intersects a newly defined, placenta-evolved regulatory mechanism. PECAM1 — 2 modalities; 17 high-confidence loci; max lead PIP 1.00; min CS = 1. PECAM1 has a large number of resolved RNA-editing and isoform-usage loci. Its placental role should be framed carefully: PECAM1 is a strong endothelial marker, but direct placental-bed studies did not support trophoblast PECAM1 as a driver of invasion or preeclampsia [A14]. The atlas signal may therefore reflect placental vascular/endothelial regulation rather than a trophoblast mechanism. HSPD1 — RNA editing; 1 high-confidence locus; lead PIP 0.994; CS = 1. HSPD1/Hsp60 is a lower-recurrence but biologically strong stress candidate. Recent work shows aberrant Hsp60 lactylation in preeclamptic trophoblasts, promoting mitochondrial fission and apoptosis [A15]. A single-variant RNA-editing QTL provides a distinct post-transcriptional layer on this mitochondrial stress pathway. 4.0.4.3 4.3 Intragenomic conflict and imprinting IGF2R — expression; 1 high-confidence locus; lead PIP 0.9992; CS = 1. IGF2R is the only one of the literature review’s six canonical conflict genes that remains high-confidence in the new run. It antagonizes IGF2 signaling and is a classic parent-of-origin growth-regulation locus [49]. Its clean single-variant expression credible set remains a compelling molecular connection between cis regulation and placental growth conflict. SGCE — isoform expression; 1 high-confidence locus; lead PIP ~1.00; CS = 1. SGCE is a new conflict-lens replacement for the prior IGF2/MEG3/PEG3/MEST/GNAS set. SGCE is maternally imprinted [A17], is expressed throughout human gestation [A16], and appears among placental imprinted genes whose expression tracks maternal one-carbon nutritional status [A18]. The resolved isoform-expression QTL therefore provides a current-run example of genetic regulation operating within an imprinted placental domain. 4.0.5 6. Synthesis The fine-mapping catalog supports three conclusions. First, fine-mapping resolution is exceptionally sharp: more than 92% of PIP≥0.9 current loci have one-variant credible sets. This creates a strong variant-prioritization resource even where biological annotation is sparse. Second, the strongest recurring biology is multi-layer RNA regulation rather than splicing alone. WSB1, SCARB2, OLAH, CTSB, GPNMB, FOLR1, GBP3 and ERAP1 recur across multiple molecular readouts, often mixing transcript abundance, isoform regulation, RNA editing, intron retention, stability, and alternative ends. This is precisely the kind of regulatory architecture that a multi-modality xQTL atlas can reveal but a standard eQTL study cannot. Third, the new run retains a coherent set of placental and pregnancy positive controls — CYP19A1, SIGLEC6, KISS1, LGALS14, PSG3/PSG9, PECAM1, HSPD1 and ERAP1 — while simultaneously weakening the prior claim that the fine-mapped catalog is dominated by canonical pregnancy GWAS and imprinted genes. The scientifically stronger interpretation is therefore that the atlas recovers known placental pathways and highlights recurrent loci whose placental role is incompletely characterized. 4.0.6 7. Limitations Current-file mismatch. The credible-set file contains 534 loci absent from the new locus summary. This review filters them out, but the report generation pipeline should be corrected so all fine-mapping products share the same run membership. PIP threshold is a statistical filter. Lead PIP ≥0.9 and a one-variant credible set are strong causal-regulatory evidence, not proof of molecular mechanism. Gene-level recurrence is not locus independence. A gene with many high-confidence molecular phenotypes can contain correlated features driven by the same underlying variant/haplotype. Bulk placenta mixes cell types. GPNMB, SCARB2 and PECAM1 illustrate why trophoblast, Hofbauer-cell and endothelial signals must be distinguished using cell-type-resolved annotations. Literature selection is illustrative. The 20 deep dives prioritize recurrence and placental interpretability; they are not the only biologically important genes among the 1,142 current high-confidence genes. Citation integration is incomplete. The original finemap_hits_evidence_table.csv was not supplied with this review. Legacy numeric citation indices are retained where possible; new sources remain [A#] until that evidence table is provided. 4.0.7 8.
