5 GWAS colocalization 5.1 Executive summary This report describes cross-ancestry colocalization between placental cis-xQTL signals and GWAS traits spanning birth weight, gestational duration, and childhood anthropometry. Colocalization is performed in a multiple-causal-signal framework: SuSiE decomposes each xQTL and GWAS locus into credible-set signals, and coloc evaluates each signal pair. The supplied aggregate contains 39,822 diagnostic attempts. After successful SuSiE signal construction and aggregation, coloc_best.tsv.gz contains 3,192 nonredundant xQTL-feature × GWAS-trait × ancestry comparisons, one row for the signal-pair with the highest PP4 in each comparison cell. Headline result. 194 comparisons are called colocalized by the supplied coloc_call flag, spanning 66 primary gene IDs, 139 molecular phenotypes, and 15 GWAS traits. Calls divide into 92 EAS and 102 EUR comparisons. Increasing the posterior threshold leaves 167 PP4 ≥ 0.80, 115 PP4 ≥ 0.90, and 87 PP4 ≥ 0.95 comparisons. The colocBoost aggregate adds 564 total colocalization-confidence-set (CoS) rows. 12 CoS events contain both placental xQTL and GWAS outcomes, representing 22 ancestry-matched gene–trait pairs across 13 genes and 12 GWAS traits. Of those pairs, 7 are also called by pairwise SuSiE-coloc and 15 are colocBoost-only, emphasizing complementarity rather than interchangeability of the two methods. The dominant regulatory layers are alternative polyadenylation, expression, and isoform expression. The strongest recurrent locus is the chromosome 17p13 region containing ELP5, CLDN7, and CTDNEP1, which colocalizes with birth-weight and early-childhood anthropometric traits through multiple placental molecular readouts. Other recurrent signals include MRPL43, PLCE1-AS1, SH3YL1, WSB1, TFPI, CTSB, and an IGF2-overlapping composite stability phenotype. No exact (modality, molecular phenotype, GWAS trait) call is shared between EAS and EUR, and no primary gene–trait call is shared across both ancestries. This is a major interpretive constraint: the atlas identifies compelling ancestry-stratified shared-signal candidates, not a catalog of cross-ancestry replicated colocalizations. 5.2 Methods 5.2.1 What SuSiE-coloc asks For a pair of association signals, the coloc posterior partitions evidence among five hypotheses: H0: neither trait is associated in the locus; H1: xQTL only; H2: GWAS only; H3: both traits are associated, but through distinct causal variants; H4: both traits are associated and share a causal variant. The quantity emphasized here is PP.H4.abf (PP4). In a SuSiE-based analysis, multiple signals can exist within each locus. Each xQTL credible set can therefore be compared with each GWAS credible set; the full CS-pair output is stored in coloc_results.tsv.gz. 5.2.2 What colocBoost adds colocBoost is a multi-trait colocalization framework that jointly models many molecular/GWAS outcomes and can accommodate multiple causal variants within a region. Its primary output is a colocalization confidence set (CoS): a set of variants and a configuration of outcomes inferred to share a causal effect. This report defines a mixed xQTL–GWAS event as a CoS whose colocalized_outcomes contains at least one placental xQTL outcome and at least one gwas: outcome. Gene–trait pairs are generated only within those mixed events. The colocBoost metrics are deliberately not converted into a PP4-like threshold. In particular, purity is an LD property of the CoS (minimum absolute within-set correlation), not a posterior probability of colocalization. cos_npc summarizes normalized colocalization support for the event, while min_npc_outcome reports the weakest normalized support among outcomes in the configuration. top_variable_vcp is the top variant’s colocalization probability. These quantities complement rather than numerically replace SuSiE-coloc PP4. 5.2.3 Why headline counts use coloc_best.tsv.gz The full aggregate has 4,314 CS-pair rows but only 3,192 unique xQTL-feature × trait × ancestry cells. Counting every CS pair as an independent biological result would inflate loci that contain multiple signals. Therefore: coloc_results.tsv.gz is used for signal-pair diagnostics; coloc_best.tsv.gz supplies one maximum-PP4 signal pair per comparison cell; all headline call counts and gene/trait summaries use coloc_best.tsv.gz. The supplied call flag is exactly equivalent to PP4 ≥ 0.7 in this aggregate. A matching lead variant (hit1 == hit2) is supportive but is not required for H4: two association signals can share a causal variant even when their marginal/credible-set lead variants differ because of LD and sampling variation. 5.2.4 Gene and trait annotation Primary gene IDs are parsed from the leading Ensembl gene ID in each molecular phenotype. If gene_map_path exists, its symbols are used. Otherwise the report falls back to Ensembl IDs plus a small curated symbol map for the most recurrent loci. JECS phenotype codes are deliberately preserved in trait labels because the aggregate files do not include a complete phenotype dictionary for every code. The report does not infer age or measurement source beyond what is explicitly encoded in the supplied IDs. 5.3 Input landscape and diagnostic funnel 5.3.1 Diagnostic outcomes status n fraction no_cs_gwas 18232 0.458 ok 15000 0.377 no_cs_xqtl 5823 0.146 too_few_variants 695 0.017 error 36 0.001 susie_fail_gwas 28 0.001 susie_fail_xqtl 8 0.000 Colocalization preparation/SuSiE diagnostic outcomes across all attempted modality–locus–trait cells. In the supplied aggregate, SH3YL1 forms an EAS event that couples multiple placental molecular modalities with four JECS childhood-BMI outcomes. PLCE1-AS1 forms another EAS event connecting isoform/poly(A) regulation with five JECS BMI outcomes. These should be interpreted as shared developmental-growth regulatory configurations, not as an equivalent number of independent causal variants. Several loci recur across multiple childhood traits or ages. PLCE1-AS1 is the broadest cross-trait example, with calls spanning birth-weight and childhood-anthropometry resources and both ancestry strata. MRPL43 and SH3YL1 each show dense, multi-modality colocalization with a single JECS BMI timepoint, whereas TFPI and CTSB carry multiple RNA-editing colocalizations with the age-10 body-size GWAS. Repeated phenotype-level calls within a gene can arise because several transcripts, editing sites, polyadenylation sites, or other features are driven by the same local haplotype. They should therefore be interpreted as evidence for a multi-feature locus, not as an equivalent number of independent causal mechanisms. 5.9 Gestational duration ancestry modality gene_label phenotype_id trait_label hit1 hit2 same_lead PP.H3.abf PP.H4.abf EUR expression NCKIPSD ENSG00000213672.8 Gestational duration — maternal GWAS (EGG 2023) 3:49163194:A:G 3:49402007:A:G FALSE 0.194135 0.700253 Gestational-duration colocalization calls. WSB1 is notable for a different reason: its five calls all connect the same fetal-birth-weight GWAS signal to five distinct placental molecular modalities (RNA editing, intron retention, isoform usage, stability, and isoform expression), giving unusually coherent multi-layer evidence. 5.11 H3 versus H4: shared versus distinct causal signals For loci in which both traits clearly associate, PP3 and PP4 are direct competitors: PP3 favors distinct causal signals, whereas PP4 favors sharing. This is why a high GWAS association signal near a strong xQTL is not sufficient for mechanistic interpretation without colocalization. Among called comparisons, 31 / 194 (16.0%) use the same lead variant for xQTL and GWAS. The majority do not, illustrating why lead-SNP matching is an inadequate substitute for LD-aware colocalization. 5.12 Cross-ancestry characterization ancestry tested_cells calls call_rate pp4_ge_0_90 EAS 2005 92 4.6% 53 EUR 1187 102 8.6% 62 Colocalization counts by ancestry. Full table is written to tables/coloc/coloc_top_calls.tsv. 5.14 Literature context The companion literature_colocalization.md reviews the strongest and most recurrent loci in the context of placental biology and previous growth GWAS / placental multi-omics work. The literature review also places the multi-trait colocBoost events in context. The strongest new external anchor is FES, which appears in a maternal-birth-weight colocBoost event and was independently prioritized by prior placental multi-omics. The SH3YL1 and PLCE1-AS1 events are emphasized as multi-timepoint developmental-growth hotspots because one CoS directly contains several JECS GWAS outcomes. The chromosome 17p13 locus is the clearest external validation point: previous placental multi-omics work independently identified CTDNEP1 as a plausible birth-weight effector at a locus where birth weight, placental DNA methylation, and placental gene expression showed colocalization. The present atlas extends that locus from total expression into multiple long-read RNA-processing phenotypes and additionally highlights ELP5 and CLDN7. 5.15 Interpretation and limitations Colocalization is not mediation. H4 supports a shared causal genetic signal; it does not establish that changing the placental molecular feature causes the GWAS phenotype. The molecular feature’s gene label is not proof of the effector gene. This is especially important in compact loci such as chr17p13. PP4 ≥0.70 is inclusive. Results above 0.90–0.95 are the strongest candidates; 0.70–0.80 calls should be viewed as suggestive. Repeated molecular features are correlated. Multiple editing sites, transcripts, polyA sites, or modalities at one locus can reflect the same underlying haplotype. No exact cross-ancestry replication is observed. Power, LD and feature detection differ by ancestry, so ancestry contrast is descriptive rather than proof of effect heterogeneity. External LD matters. The project pipeline uses ancestry-matched 1000 Genomes LD for the SuSiE-coloc stage; mismatch between the LD reference and the underlying xQTL/GWAS study populations can alter signal decomposition. Aggregate outputs do not contain all harmonization details. Allele alignment and effect-direction auditing belong in the pipeline QC, not in this descriptive aggregate report. colocBoost evidence metrics are not PP4. purity describes within-CoS LD coherence; cos_npc, min_npc_outcome, and variant VCP carry different meanings and should not be thresholded or narrated as if they were Bayesian PP4 values. Pairwise and multi-trait non-overlap is expected. A colocBoost-only event can arise because joint modeling borrows configuration information across several outcomes or resolves multiple effects differently; it is not automatically a contradiction of SuSiE-coloc. Trait availability is uneven. The catalog is conditional on the GWAS traits included in this run and should not be interpreted as a comprehensive survey of pregnancy or childhood phenotypes. JECS codes are preserved. Exact timepoint semantics should be taken from the original GWAS phenotype dictionary before manuscript-level naming. 5.16 Reproducibility The report writes reusable derived tables to: tables/coloc/coloc_calls.tsv tables/coloc/coloc_gene_summary.tsv tables/coloc/coloc_trait_summary.tsv tables/coloc/coloc_modality_summary.tsv tables/coloc/coloc_diagnostics_pivot.tsv tables/coloc/coloc_top_calls.tsv tables/coloc/colocboost_mixed_events.tsv (when colocBoost input is available) tables/coloc/colocboost_gene_trait_pairs.tsv (when colocBoost input is available) and figures to figures/coloc/. item path exists Resolved coloc directory /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/coloc/aggregated TRUE Best comparisons /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/coloc/aggregated/coloc_best.tsv.gz TRUE All CS pairs /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/coloc/aggregated/coloc_results.tsv.gz TRUE Diagnostics /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/coloc/aggregated/coloc_diagnostics_summary.tsv TRUE colocBoost clusters /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/coloc/aggregated/colocboost_clusters.tsv.gz TRUE Gene map /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/placenta_xqtl_report_inputs_20261010/gene_map.tsv TRUE Resolved report inputs. ## 6 Literature context: colocalization findings

6 Literature context: colocalization findings Project: Placenta xQTL atlas Companion report: report_colocalization.Rmd / rendered report_colocalization.html Results basis: coloc_best.tsv.gz, coloc_results.tsv.gz, coloc_diagnostics_summary.tsv, and colocboost_clusters.tsv.gz from the supplied colocalization aggregate. Bracketed references [1]–[14] resolve to coloc_hits_evidence_table.csv, retained from the archived report convention. References [15]–[17] below cover the colocBoost additions and new interpretation. 6.0.1 1. Scope and interpretation The colocalization analysis asks whether a placental molecular QTL and an external GWAS association are statistically consistent with a shared causal variant rather than merely occupying the same genomic neighborhood. The pipeline uses the SuSiE extension of coloc, which permits multiple causal signals within a locus and evaluates pairs of resolved signals rather than assuming one causal variant per region [1]. The supplied nonredundant coloc_best.tsv.gz contains 3,192 xQTL-feature × GWAS-trait × ancestry comparison cells. 194 are called colocalized by the supplied flag (which corresponds to PP4 ≥0.70 in these files), with 167 at PP4 ≥0.80, 115 at PP4 ≥0.90, and 87 at PP4 ≥0.95. The called set spans 139 molecular phenotypes, 66 primary Ensembl gene IDs, and 15 GWAS traits. There are 92 EAS and 102 EUR calls. The trait panel covers four related but genetically distinct early-growth settings. The 2019 EGG analyses distinguish direct fetal, indirect maternal, and own-birth-weight genetic effects [2]. The age-10 body-size GWAS is a UK Biobank measure of comparative childhood body size [3]. The JECS data provide dense early-childhood anthropometric GWAS in a Japanese birth cohort [4], and the maternal gestational-duration GWAS comes from the 2023 EGG meta-analysis [5]. These distinctions matter: a placental xQTL that colocalizes with fetal birth weight and one that colocalizes with a maternal birth-weight effect do not have the same causal interpretation. This review focuses on loci, not raw row counts. Several molecular phenotypes from one gene—and several neighboring genes—can be driven by the same local haplotype. Repeated colocalization across transcripts, poly(A) sites, editing sites, or modalities is therefore evidence of a coherent regulatory hotspot, not proof of multiple independent causal mechanisms. 6.0.2 2. Overview of the result landscape The 194 calls are concentrated in alternative polyadenylation (53), expression (44), and isoform expression (43), followed by RNA editing (16), stability (12), isoform usage (11), intron retention (9), and alternative TSS (6). No splicing comparison is called in the current aggregate. Because the diagnostic funnel contains very few successfully resolved splicing comparisons, this absence should not be interpreted as a biological exclusion of splicing. The GWAS side is dominated by developmental anthropometric phenotypes: comparative body size at age 10 contributes 70 calls; fetal/direct birth weight contributes 24; several JECS BMI timepoints contribute substantial additional counts; own birth weight contributes 11; and the maternal birth-weight and maternal gestational-duration resources contribute smaller sets. Only 31/194 called comparisons use the identical xQTL and GWAS lead variant. This is expected under LD-aware colocalization: H4 concerns a shared causal signal, not equality of the marginal lead SNP. The most important negative result is cross-ancestry replication. No exact molecular-feature–trait call, and no primary gene–trait call, reaches the colocalization criterion in both EAS and EUR. This makes the current atlas a set of ancestry-stratified mechanistic hypotheses rather than internally replicated trans-ancestry colocalizations. 6.0.3 2.1 What colocBoost adds to the pairwise catalog The archived report was based on pairwise SuSiE-coloc. The new colocboost_clusters.tsv.gz adds a different view: joint multi-trait colocalization. ColocBoost uses a multi-task gradient-boosting framework that can accommodate multiple causal variants and discover configurations of several outcomes sharing one effect. Each event is represented by a colocalization confidence set (CoS) of candidate variants and a set of colocalized outcomes [15,16]. The supplied colocBoost aggregate contains 564 CoS rows. Of these, 12 events jointly contain at least one placental xQTL and at least one GWAS outcome. Those events yield 22 ancestry-matched gene–trait pairs involving 13 genes and 12 GWAS traits. Seven of the 22 pairs are also called by pairwise SuSiE-coloc in the same ancestry; 15 are colocBoost-only. This is not an “agreement rate” in the conventional sense because the methods have different targets and signal decompositions. The overlap is best used as a high-confidence convergence tier; colocBoost-only events are complementary multi-trait hypotheses. The 12 mixed events have high LD coherence overall (median CoS purity ~0.974), but purity is not a posterior probability. In the colocBoost output, purity is the minimum absolute correlation among variants in the CoS, top_variable_vcp is the top variant’s colocalization probability, cos_npc summarizes normalized colocalization support for the event, and min_npc_outcome is the weakest normalized support among its outcomes [16]. Two events are especially informative for developmental trajectories. A SH3YL1 EAS event jointly links seven placental xQTL outcomes across expression/isoform/poly(A)/stability layers with four JECS BMI GWAS outcomes (Dr1m, C1Y_1, C3Y and C4Y). A PLCE1-AS1 EAS event links isoform/poly(A) regulation with five JECS BMI outcomes (Dr1m, C6m, C1Y_1, C1Y_2 and C3HY). The appropriate interpretation is a shared regulatory configuration across several growth timepoints, not four or five independent causal variants. Other mixed events implicate FAP, C3orf38, FES, FUBP1, GCLM, MRPL18/TCP1, BCKDHB, RBIS, ARF4, and NPEPL1. These provide a compact shortlist for follow-up because the xQTL and GWAS outcomes were selected jointly rather than by repeated pairwise scanning. 6.0.4 3. The chr17p13 birth-weight hotspot: ELP5, CLDN7 and CTDNEP1 The strongest and best externally validated locus in the results lies at 17p13, where ELP5, CLDN7 and CTDNEP1 sit within a compact regulatory region. 6.0.4.1 3.1 ELP5: the dominant molecular-feature signal ELP5 accounts for 29 called comparison rows, the largest count for any primary gene ID. In EUR, the fetal/direct birth-weight GWAS colocalizes with ELP5 expression, isoform expression, isoform usage, and multiple alternative-polyadenylation phenotypes, many with PP4 ~0.995–1.00. Several of these comparisons use the same xQTL and GWAS lead variant 17:7259132:G:A. In EAS, ELP5 poly(A), isoform-expression, and isoform-usage signals colocalize with trans-ancestry own birth weight, JECS low birth weight, and neonatal/early-childhood BMI codes. ELP5 itself is a component of the Elongator complex and is annotated for tRNA modification and cell-migration biology [8]. It does not yet have a strong placenta-specific disease literature. Consequently, the strength of the ELP5 signal comes primarily from genetic convergence across molecular modalities and growth traits, not from prior mechanistic expectation. 6.0.4.2 3.2 CLDN7: an independently recognizable birth-weight region CLDN7 has four EUR fetal-birth-weight calls across expression and alternative-polyadenylation phenotypes. The strongest has PP4 ~0.9998, and the same 17:7259132:G:A variant is the xQTL and GWAS lead in several comparisons. CLDN7 encodes a tight-junction claudin at 17p13.1 [14]. Importantly, the region is not novel to birth-weight genetics. Fine-mapping in the Black Women’s Health Study previously evaluated a SLC2A4/CLDN7 17p13 birth-weight locus [7]. Thus the present placental xQTL colocalization places a molecular regulatory readout directly under a previously recognized birth-weight association region. 6.0.4.3 3.3 CTDNEP1: direct replication of prior placental multi-omics CTDNEP1 provides the strongest external validation of the atlas’s biological interpretation. In the results, an EAS CTDNEP1 intron-retention phenotype colocalizes with trans-ancestry own birth weight (PP4 ~0.967) and with JECS Dr0m/Dr1m BMI signals. A prior placental multi-omics study integrated birth-weight GWAS, placental DNA methylation, and placental gene expression and independently highlighted CTDNEP1 at chr17p13. That study found evidence for shared genetic architecture linking birth weight, placental methylation, and CTDNEP1-related expression at the locus, and identified CTDNEP1 among candidate functional birth-weight genes [6]. The present atlas therefore does not merely rediscover a nearby GWAS peak: it extends a previously implicated placental locus into RNA-processing regulation, particularly intron retention. 6.0.4.4 3.4 Interpretation of the hotspot ELP5, CLDN7 and CTDNEP1 should not be presented as three independent causal genes solely because all appear in the call table. Their physical proximity, shared lead variants, and overlapping trait associations make the more defensible interpretation a chr17p13 placental regulatory hotspot. The current data nominate several candidate molecular consequences within that hotspot; distinguishing the true effector gene(s) will require conditional analyses, variant-level functional annotation, and experimental perturbation. 6.0.5 4. WSB1: five molecular routes to fetal birth weight WSB1 is one of the cleanest multi-modality colocalizations outside chr17p13. Five EUR molecular phenotypes—RNA editing, intron retention, isoform usage, transcript stability, and isoform expression—colocalize with the EGG fetal/direct birth-weight signal at PP4 ~0.997. In every one of these comparisons, the same lead variant (17:27310317:G:A) is selected for the xQTL and GWAS signal. WSB1 has a plausible placental stress biology even though it has not been established as a canonical birth-weight gene. It encodes the substrate-recognition component of an E3 ubiquitin ligase, is a HIF-1 target, regulates proteins involved in hypoxic responses, and produces multiple functional transcripts; earlier tissue profiling reported WSB1 transcripts in placenta [9]. This makes the locus particularly attractive: the colocalization links a fetal-growth GWAS signal to five distinct placental RNA phenotypes at a gene already positioned in hypoxia-responsive biology. The data do not establish which RNA phenotype mediates fetal growth. Rather, they show that a single fetal-birth-weight locus has unusually coherent effects across WSB1 RNA processing. 6.0.6 5. PLCE1-AS1: a cross-trait developmental-growth locus PLCE1-AS1 has 11 calls spanning seven traits, three molecular modalities, and both ancestry strata, making it the widest cross-trait locus in the current catalog. EUR signals include fetal/direct birth weight, maternal birth weight, and comparative body size at age 10; EAS signals include several JECS BMI timepoints. The molecular phenotypes include alternative polyadenylation, isoform expression, and stability. PLCE1-AS1 is a validated antisense noncoding RNA with detectable expression in placenta [10], but there is little direct literature tying it to placental growth regulation. That combination—broad developmental-trait recurrence, cross-ancestry appearance at different trait comparisons, and sparse prior placental mechanism—makes it one of the atlas’s stronger novel developmental-regulation candidates. The recurrence should not be read as proof of one causal pathway from birth weight to later BMI. These are separate GWAS traits. The result instead suggests that genetic variation at the PLCE1-AS1 locus intersects several stages of growth and body-size biology. 6.0.7 6. Dense single-trait regulatory hotspots 6.0.7.1 6.1 MRPL43 and JECS C1Y_2 MRPL43 contributes 16 EAS calls, all to one JECS childhood-BMI code (C1Y_2), but distributed across four molecular modalities: alternative polyadenylation, intron retention, isoform expression, and isoform usage. The maximum PP4 is ~0.954. The concentration of many RNA features on one GWAS signal suggests a broad post-transcriptional regulatory haplotype rather than 16 independent mechanisms. MRPL43 encodes a mitochondrial ribosomal protein; the current literature search did not identify direct evidence that MRPL43 itself is a placental childhood-growth effector. This is therefore a strong genetic signal with comparatively weak prior biological annotation. 6.0.7.2 6.2 SH3YL1 and JECS C6m SH3YL1 contributes seven EAS calls to JECS C6m BMI across five modalities: alternative polyadenylation, expression, stability, isoform expression, and isoform usage. PP4 reaches ~0.912. As with MRPL43, the scientific value lies in cross-modality consistency at one locus. The result nominates SH3YL1-associated RNA regulation during a period of rapid infant growth, but direct placental mechanistic evidence remains limited. It is a candidate for follow-up rather than a known positive control. The colocBoost result materially strengthens the locus-level case for SH3YL1. Rather than connecting the locus to only one JECS timepoint at a time, the same EAS CoS includes four childhood-BMI GWAS outcomes and multiple placental molecular readouts. This does not prove one biological effect persists unchanged across childhood, but it supports a parsimonious shared developmental-growth signal. 6.0.8 7. RNA-editing colocalizations with childhood body size RNA editing is a comparatively small component of the total call set, but it contains several highly interpretable recurrent loci for the age-10 body-size GWAS. 6.0.8.1 7.1 TFPI Four EUR TFPI editing sites colocalize with comparative body size at age 10; the strongest PP4 is ~0.963. TFPI is biologically notable because it is highly expressed in placenta and sits in the coagulation pathway. Circulating TFPI has also been reported to rise before clinical preeclampsia and in established disease [11]. The colocalization trait here is childhood body size, not preeclampsia. Thus the pregnancy literature supports placental plausibility but does not demonstrate the mechanism connecting TFPI editing to later body size. The novel observation is that a childhood anthropometric GWAS signal shares genetic architecture with specific placental TFPI RNA-editing phenotypes. 6.0.8.2 7.2 CTSB Four EUR CTSB editing sites also colocalize with the age-10 body-size GWAS, with PP4 up to ~0.994. Cathepsin B has stronger trophoblast context than many editing hits: experimental trophoblast work links CTSB expression to beta-catenin-dependent migration/invasion under a preeclampsia-relevant hypoxia framework [12]. Again, the result should not be overextended to disease causality. It provides a candidate bridge between a placental invasion/proteolysis gene and later body-size genetics through a post-transcriptional editing phenotype. 6.0.9 8. The IGF2-overlapping composite stability phenotype One of the most biologically provocative EAS signals is a composite stability phenotype labeled ENSG00000240801.1_ENSG00000284779.3. It colocalizes with JECS C6m, Dr0m, and Dr1m BMI; the strongest comparison has PP4 ~0.972 and uses the same xQTL and GWAS lead variant (11:2146751:G:A). This phenotype must be described carefully. The first Ensembl ID corresponds to an IGF2-overlapping noncoding locus, but the phenotype ID is composite; it should not be renamed as an IGF2 QTL without checking its construction. Nevertheless, its genomic context is compelling because placental IGF2 is a canonical regulator of placental and fetal growth. Experimental deletion of a placenta-specific Igf2 transcript reduces placental growth and subsequently causes fetal growth restriction [13]. The colocalization therefore merits targeted annotation of the underlying stability phenotype and its transcript boundaries. It is a good example of where the long-read/derived phenotype definition matters as much as the gene-level label. 6.0.10 9. SLC6A2 and neonatal JECS BMI SLC6A2 has four EAS alternative-polyadenylation calls with the JECS Dr0m BMI trait, all with PP4 >0.96 and a common GWAS lead. This is a highly resolved 3’-end-regulation signal, but the targeted literature search did not identify strong evidence for SLC6A2 as a known placental growth gene. Accordingly, this locus belongs in the novel-mechanism category. The specificity for alternative polyadenylation is useful: rather than simply nominating SLC6A2 expression, the atlas points to 3’-end choice as the molecular phenotype most consistent with the GWAS signal. 6.0.11 10. Gestational duration: one borderline signal Only one called comparison involves the 2023 maternal gestational-duration GWAS: EUR NCKIPSD expression, with PP4 ~0.7003. The EGG resource is a large maternal meta-analysis of gestational duration [5], but the atlas posterior is essentially at the inclusive call threshold. This signal should therefore be reported as suggestive/provisional, not as a core colocalization result. A higher PP4 threshold would remove it. 6.0.12 10.1 New colocBoost-prioritized loci 6.0.12.1 FES and maternal birth weight The FES mixed event is one of the strongest external-validation additions. In EUR, FES expression and isoform expression colocalize jointly with the EGG maternal-birth-weight GWAS in a one-variant CoS. This is important because an independent placental multi-omics study previously used multi-trait colocalization to prioritize FES as a likely functional effector for birth weight [6]. The current result therefore recovers FES through a different placental molecular dataset and a different multi-trait colocalization framework. Notably, FES is not significant in the current gene-level TWAS for maternal birth weight. That discrepancy is scientifically useful: it demonstrates that prediction-based association and shared-signal inference are complementary rather than interchangeable. 6.0.12.2 FAP and decidual remodeling An EAS FAP expression/isoform event colocalizes with a JECS early-childhood BMI outcome. FAP has direct pregnancy context: fibroblast activation protein is expressed on decidual stromal fibroblasts during early pregnancy and has been implicated in physiological tissue remodeling [17]. The growth connection is not established in prior literature, so this remains a novel mechanistic hypothesis, but it is more interpretable than an unannotated locus because the gene maps to a placenta-relevant stromal process. 6.0.12.3 C3orf38 and age-10 body size The EUR C3orf38 event colocalizes with comparative body size at age 10 and is also supported by pairwise SuSiE-coloc. The same gene–trait pair is strongly significant in the current TWAS, creating three-way statistical convergence. Direct placental/growth biology for C3orf38 remains sparse; accordingly, it should be highlighted as a high-priority novel candidate rather than assigned a mechanism prematurely. 6.0.12.4 Remaining colocBoost-only configurations GCLM, MRPL18/TCP1, BCKDHB, RBIS, ARF4, and NPEPL1 occur in mixed events that are absent from the pairwise call set for at least some represented gene–trait pairs. These are best treated as a secondary discovery tier pending locus-level inspection. Their value lies in joint configuration support across outcomes, while the absence of pairwise PP4 support argues for additional sensitivity analysis before mechanistic claims. 6.0.13 11. Cross-cutting interpretation 6.0.13.1 11.1 Placental RNA processing, not only total expression, links to growth GWAS The largest call class is alternative polyadenylation, and many flagship loci are supported simultaneously by isoform expression, isoform usage, editing, intron retention, or stability. The key contribution of this atlas is therefore not simply another placental eQTL–GWAS colocalization scan. It resolves which layer of RNA regulation shares genetic architecture with a developmental trait. The chr17p13 locus is the clearest example: prior placental multi-omics already implicated CTDNEP1 and nearby regulatory signals in birth weight [6], whereas the present analysis reveals a much wider spectrum of placental RNA-processing phenotypes across CTDNEP1, ELP5 and CLDN7. 6.0.13.2 11.2 Birth weight and childhood size share recurrent loci, but not necessarily one pathway ELP5/chr17p13 and PLCE1-AS1 recur across birth-weight and childhood-BMI/body-size resources. This supports developmental continuity at the level of genetic loci, but it does not show that placental regulation mediates a causal path from birth weight to later adiposity. Formal mediation or multivariable causal analyses would be needed for that conclusion. 6.0.13.3 11.3 Exact cross-ancestry replication is absent Despite 194 calls, no exact gene–trait pair is called in both EAS and EUR. That absence may reflect real ancestry differences, but several technical and statistical explanations are equally plausible: different LD structure, allele frequency, xQTL power, molecular-feature detection, and GWAS ancestry. The strongest way to use the multi-ancestry design at this stage is therefore to ask whether loci and pathways recur across ancestries, while keeping exact PP4 calls ancestry-specific. 6.0.14 12. Limitations PP4 is evidence for shared genetic causality, not molecular mediation. A colocalized xQTL can be a correlated readout of the causal regulatory process rather than the mediator itself. Gene attribution is phenotype-based. Neighboring genes at a compact locus can all inherit evidence from the same haplotype. PP4 ≥0.70 is permissive. The 0.90–0.95 subset is a more conservative shortlist. Repeated molecular phenotypes are correlated. Row counts should not be interpreted as counts of independent causal variants. No exact cross-ancestry replication is present. The LD reference can influence SuSiE decomposition. The project uses ancestry-matched 1000 Genomes LD rather than the original GWAS individual genotypes. The aggregate does not expose all harmonization/QC fields. Variant alignment and per-locus LD diagnostics must be audited upstream. JECS labels are source codes. A final manuscript should replace codes such as Dr0m, C1Y_2, and C3HY with definitions from the original phenotype dictionary. Literature absence is search-dependent. “Novel” here means no compelling direct placental/growth mechanism was identified in the targeted searches, not proof that none exists. 6.0.15 13. Synthesis The addition of colocBoost changes the interpretation from a purely pairwise catalog to a pairwise-plus-multi-trait atlas. SuSiE-coloc remains the clearest per-feature/per-GWAS posterior framework, while colocBoost reveals configurations that span several molecular modalities and several GWAS timepoints. The strongest candidates are those that converge across methods; the most interesting novel candidates are colocBoost-only events with coherent placental biology or TWAS support. Three findings stand out. First, chr17p13 is a compelling positive-validation locus. Birth-weight genetics previously implicated the SLC2A4/CLDN7 region [7], and independent placental multi-omics prioritized CTDNEP1 at the same locus [6]. The current atlas adds near-certain ELP5/CLDN7 colocalizations and CTDNEP1 RNA-processing signals, strongly supporting a placenta-relevant regulatory hotspot. Second, multi-modality convergence identifies candidates that conventional eQTL analysis would understate. WSB1 is the cleanest example, with one fetal birth-weight signal colocalizing across five RNA-processing layers. MRPL43 and SH3YL1 show similarly broad molecular effects for individual JECS BMI timepoints. Third, the catalog suggests genetic continuity between placental regulation and postnatal anthropometry, particularly at PLCE1-AS1, TFPI, CTSB, and several JECS-linked loci. These observations are hypotheses about shared genetic architecture—not proof of developmental mediation—but they create a focused set of variants and molecular phenotypes for the next stage of causal and functional work. 6.0.16 14. 7 Transcriptome-wide association study 7.1 Executive summary This report summarizes placental transcriptome-wide association testing performed with FUSION prediction weights at both gene and isoform resolution. The supplied aggregate contains 258,124 model-level tests representing 8,075 primary Ensembl genes across 16 GWAS traits, together with 131,523 gene-level ACAT aggregation rows. Headline result. At the supplied false-discovery threshold, 3,041 model-level associations have TWAS.Q < 0.05, and 2,098 gene × trait × weight-set rows have acat_q < 0.05. The gene-level set corresponds to 2,032 distinct gene–trait combinations before collapsing weight sets. Among significant TWAS gene–trait pairs, 31 are also represented by a called SuSiE-coloc gene–trait pair and 12 by a mixed xQTL–GWAS colocBoost event; 40 have support from at least one colocalization framework. The recurrent TWAS landscape contains both well-established body-weight genes—most prominently ADCY3, LEP, and LEPR—and placenta-centered candidates such as ELP5, CLDN7, CTDNEP1, SLC38A1, FAP, PLCE1-AS1, and SH3YL1. TWAS should be interpreted as evidence that the genetically predicted placental molecular phenotype is associated with the GWAS trait; it is not by itself proof of mediation or of a unique causal gene. 7.2 Methods 7.2.1 FUSION model-level tests FUSION predicts the genetically regulated component of a molecular phenotype from cis-genetic weights and tests that predicted component against GWAS summary statistics. Here the ID field includes both gene models and long-read isoform models. A model is classified as isoform-level when its identifier contains __; otherwise it is classified as a gene-level model. The report treats the supplied TWAS.P and TWAS.Q values as authoritative. Because a small number of extremely significant p-values are stored as numeric zero, all plotting code floors p-values at .Machine$double.xmin before -log10 transformation; the underlying result tables are not altered. 7.2.2 Gene-level ACAT aggregation twas_gene_results.tsv.gz combines the available gene and isoform model p-values for each gene × trait × weight-set cell with ACAT. acat_q is used for headline gene-level discovery. The ACAT statistic is direction-free; when this report displays a direction it explicitly labels it as the lead model TWAS Z, not a gene-level ACAT effect direction. 7.2.3 Prediction weight sets weight_set denotes the placental prediction-weight panel (EAS, EUR, or pooled). It should not be read as a balanced replication design. The external GWAS resources available to each ancestry differ substantially, so raw EAS-versus-EUR hit counts are not directly comparable. These genes provide strong biological face validity for the anthropometric GWAS panel, while their appearance in a placental TWAS does not imply that the known central-nervous-system or systemic mechanisms of obesity operate exclusively through placenta. 7.6 Gene versus isoform signal Because multiple gene and isoform models can represent the same primary gene and are correlated through local LD, raw model counts are not independent biological discoveries. The gene-level ACAT layer is therefore the preferred primary summary; model-level results are most useful for identifying which transcript model drives a gene-level association. 7.7 Cross-weight-set concordance comparison n_shared_models sign_concordance spearman_rho EAS vs pooled 31809 71.7% 0.586 EUR vs pooled 1837 64.9% 0.418 Direction/rank concordance for exact trait + model IDs shared between ancestry-specific and pooled prediction weights. The shared-model comparisons are not independent replications because pooled weights are trained using overlapping information and the trait coverage is uneven. They are nevertheless a useful stability check: concordant signs indicate that the predicted molecular phenotype is generally oriented similarly when the same model/trait combination can be evaluated. 7.8 Integration with colocalization TWAS and colocalization answer different questions. TWAS tests association of a genetically predicted placental molecular phenotype with a GWAS trait. SuSiE-coloc asks whether the xQTL and GWAS are consistent with a shared causal signal. colocBoost jointly searches for multi-trait colocalization events. Convergence therefore raises priority, while lack of colocalization does not automatically invalidate a TWAS association. ## Among significant TWAS gene–trait pairs, 31 overlap a called SuSiE-coloc ADCY3, LEP, and LEPR are notable because human genetic evidence independently establishes roles in body-weight regulation. Their recurrence across multiple childhood traits supports the biological calibration of the TWAS panel, but these loci should not be described as placenta-specific without additional tissue-comparison analyses. 7.11 Literature context The companion literature_twas.md reviews the TWAS architecture and the strongest convergent loci in the context of previous placental transcriptomics, placental multi-omics, nutrient transport, and obesity genetics. It also distinguishes three evidence tiers useful for manuscript writing: TWAS + colocalization + prior placental evidence (highest mechanistic priority); TWAS + colocalization with limited prior placental literature (novel atlas-driven candidates); recurrent TWAS without colocalization (association candidates requiring stronger causal disambiguation). 7.12 Interpretation and limitations TWAS association is not mediation. A significant result can arise from shared LD or horizontally pleiotropic genetic effects and does not prove that the placental molecular phenotype mediates the GWAS association. ACAT is direction-free. Gene-level ACAT combines model p-values; any displayed TWAS Z belongs to the lead component model, not to the ACAT aggregate itself. Gene and isoform models are correlated. Multiple significant transcript models from one locus should not be counted as independent biological mechanisms. Prediction quality varies. MODELCV.R2 should accompany interpretation of individual models, particularly ancestry-specific models with smaller training sets. Weight-set coverage is unbalanced across GWAS resources. EAS/EUR discovery counts are not a formal replication comparison. Very small p-values underflow to zero. This affects display precision but not the conclusion that these are extremely significant associations. Colocalization is complementary. TWAS can be significant without a called coloc event and vice versa; each method has distinct power and modeling assumptions. Placental specificity is not established by this report. Some recurrent genes (for example ADCY3, LEP, LEPR) have important biology in other tissues; tissue-specific causal claims require external comparison. GWAS trait semantics matter. Maternal and fetal birth-weight effects, gestational duration, and childhood body-size/BMI phenotypes have distinct causal interpretations. 7.13 Reproducibility Rendering writes reusable derived tables to: tables/twas/twas_testing_coverage.tsv tables/twas/twas_model_class_summary.tsv tables/twas/twas_trait_summary.tsv tables/twas/twas_significant_genes.tsv tables/twas/twas_significant_models.tsv tables/twas/twas_recurrent_genes.tsv tables/twas/twas_coloc_prioritized.tsv tables/twas/twas_weightset_concordance.tsv and figures to figures/twas/. item path exists Resolved TWAS directory /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/coloc/aggregated TRUE Gene aggregate /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/coloc/aggregated/twas_gene_results.tsv.gz TRUE Model aggregate /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/coloc/aggregated/twas_results.tsv.gz TRUE Gene map /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/placenta_xqtl_report_inputs_20261010/gene_map.tsv TRUE SuSiE-coloc best /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/coloc/aggregated/coloc_best.tsv.gz TRUE colocBoost clusters /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/coloc/aggregated/colocboost_clusters.tsv.gz TRUE Resolved report inputs. ## 8 Literature context: TWAS findings

8 Literature context: TWAS findings Project: Placenta xQTL atlas Companion report: report_twas.Rmd / rendered report_twas.html Results basis: twas_results.tsv.gz and twas_gene_results.tsv.gz, with optional integration of coloc_best.tsv.gz and colocboost_clusters.tsv.gz. 8.0.1 1. Scope and interpretation The TWAS layer asks whether the genetically predicted component of a placental molecular phenotype is associated with an external GWAS trait. The implementation uses FUSION-style predictive weights for both gene-level and long-read isoform phenotypes. FUSION explicitly frames TWAS as prediction of the genetic component of a functional phenotype followed by association testing against GWAS summary statistics [1]. The supplied aggregate contains 258,124 model-level tests and 131,523 gene-level ACAT rows across 16 growth-related GWAS traits. At the supplied multiple-testing thresholds, 3,041 model rows have TWAS.Q < 0.05 and 2,098 gene × trait × weight-set rows have acat_q < 0.05. The gene-level layer uses the Cauchy combination test (ACAT), which provides a computationally efficient way to combine dependent p-values [2]. In this application, ACAT is useful because multiple gene and isoform prediction models can exist for the same primary gene. These results require the standard TWAS caution: association of predicted placental expression or isoform abundance with a phenotype does not by itself establish mediation. A TWAS signal can reflect LD between causal variants, shared genetic regulation, or pleiotropy. Colocalization is therefore used as an orthogonal prioritization layer rather than as a redundant significance test [3]. 8.0.2 2. Overall architecture of the current TWAS The model-level result set contains 8,075 primary Ensembl genes. Prediction weights are unevenly distributed across ancestry panels: approximately two thirds of model tests use pooled weights, with a much larger EAS-specific than EUR-specific component among the remaining tests. The imbalance largely reflects the GWAS resources available for each ancestry: the Japanese JECS childhood traits have extensive EAS-weight testing but almost no EUR-weight testing, whereas the age-10 comparative body-size GWAS has broad EUR-weight testing but essentially no EAS-weight coverage. This design means that raw EAS-versus-EUR discovery counts are not a replication experiment. Pooled weights provide the broadest cross-trait view, while ancestry-specific weights are most informative when the corresponding external GWAS is well matched. The median cross-validated prediction R² across model-level tests is about 0.025. Isoform models are numerous and contribute substantially to discovery. This is scientifically useful because long-read transcript architecture can localize a locus to a particular transcript model, but significant transcript models from the same gene are correlated and should not be counted as independent genes or mechanisms. 8.0.3 3. Recurrent body-weight genes provide biological calibration 8.0.3.1 3.1 ADCY3 ADCY3 is the broadest recurrent gene-level TWAS signal in the current aggregate: it is significant across ten GWAS traits and more than one weight set. This is a strong biological calibration point. Independent human genetics established that rare loss-of-function mutations in ADCY3 can cause severe monogenic obesity, while other loss-of-function variants increase risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes [4,5]. The relevant caution is tissue interpretation. ADCY3 has well-established roles in neuronal ciliary signaling and energy balance; a placental TWAS association therefore does not imply that the known obesity mechanism is placental. Instead, the result shows that cis-genetic predictors learned in placenta track anthropometric GWAS signal at a canonical body-weight locus. Tissue-comparison or colocalization analyses are needed before claiming a placenta-specific effector route. 8.0.3.2 3.2 LEP and LEPR LEP is significant for ten childhood-BMI traits in the supplied gene aggregate, and LEPR for nine. The leptin pathway is central to body-weight regulation, but it is also directly relevant to pregnancy: human placenta expresses leptin and leptin receptors, and placental leptin has long been proposed to participate in fetal growth, trophoblast biology, and maternal metabolic adaptation [6,7]. The recurrence of both ligand and receptor across childhood anthropometric phenotypes is therefore biologically coherent. It should nevertheless be described as convergence on a known metabolic pathway rather than proof that placental leptin signaling mediates later childhood BMI. 8.0.4 4. Placenta-specific precedent: CLDN7 and the 17p13 growth locus A key strength of the atlas is that several TWAS signals fall in loci already implicated by placental functional genomics. Peng and colleagues used placental transcriptome data to show that genetically regulated placental expression underlies birth weight and childhood obesity risk; their results included the SLC2A4/CLDN7 region among birth-weight-linked placental expression signals [8]. In the present aggregate, CLDN7 is significant for fetal/direct birth weight, JECS low birth weight, neonatal BMI, and a later infant BMI trait. The corresponding chr17p13 region is also one of the strongest xQTL–GWAS colocalization hotspots in the atlas. This convergence is more persuasive than TWAS alone because it links (i) prior placental transcriptomic evidence, (ii) the current genetically predicted placental phenotype, and (iii) shared-signal colocalization. The same compact region contains ELP5 and CTDNEP1, so gene-level assignment remains nontrivial. The locus is best presented as a regulatory hotspot whose candidate effector genes can be ranked by orthogonal evidence rather than as several independent causal genes. 8.0.5 5. CTDNEP1: convergence with prior placental multi-omics CTDNEP1 is significant in the current TWAS for fetal/direct birth weight and a neonatal BMI phenotype. A 2022 placental multi-omics study integrating birth-weight GWAS with placental methylation and expression independently identified CTDNEP1 among candidate functional birth-weight genes [9]. That study also used multi-trait colocalization to prioritize placental effector genes. This prior evidence substantially strengthens the current CTDNEP1 TWAS interpretation. The novel contribution of the present atlas is that CTDNEP1 sits within a much richer RNA-regulatory context, including xQTL signals beyond conventional total expression. 8.0.6 6. SLC38A1 connects genetic association to placental nutrient transport SLC38A1 encodes SNAT1, one of the three System A neutral amino-acid transporters expressed in human placenta. Placental System A/L activity is closely linked to fetal growth: reduced activity is associated with fetal growth restriction, while increased activity has been linked to fetal overgrowth [10,11]. The strongest current SLC38A1 TWAS association is with a neonatal/early-childhood BMI trait and is significant with both EAS and pooled weights. It also has SuSiE-coloc support in the atlas. This makes SLC38A1 a particularly interpretable candidate because the statistical evidence lands on a pathway with a direct physiological route—maternal-to-fetal nutrient transfer—rather than on a gene with only generic developmental annotation. The inference should remain precise: the data support a genetically linked placental SLC38A1 molecular phenotype at a growth-associated locus; they do not establish that altered SNAT1 transport is the causal mediator in these individuals. 8.0.7 7. FAP: a novel growth association with decidual-remodeling context FAP is one of the most recurrent gene-level TWAS signals, significant across nine traits and more than one weight set. It is additionally involved in a mixed EAS xQTL–GWAS colocBoost event for a JECS childhood-BMI phenotype. FAP is not a canonical childhood-obesity gene, but there is pregnancy-specific biological context: fibroblast activation protein is strongly expressed on decidual stromal fibroblasts in early pregnancy and has been proposed to facilitate physiological tissue remodeling during decidualization [12]. The current TWAS/colocalization convergence therefore nominates a plausible stromal-remodeling route that would not have been obvious from anthropometric GWAS alone. This is an example of an atlas-driven candidate where the placental biology is plausible but the specific link to childhood growth remains novel and requires functional follow-up. 8.0.8 8. PLCE1-AS1 and SH3YL1: recurrent developmental-growth loci strengthened by colocBoost PLCE1-AS1 is significant across ten GWAS traits in the current TWAS and is one of the broadest loci in the pairwise colocalization catalog. colocBoost adds an important multi-trait observation: one EAS colocalization confidence set jointly connects PLCE1-AS1 isoform/poly(A) regulation with five JECS childhood-BMI GWAS outcomes. Several of those gene–trait pairs are also TWAS significant. SH3YL1 is significant across nine traits. colocBoost identifies a single EAS multi-trait event connecting multiple SH3YL1 molecular modalities with four JECS BMI outcomes. This pattern is more parsimoniously interpreted as a shared developmental-growth regulatory locus than as four independent GWAS/TWAS mechanisms. Direct placenta-specific literature for PLCE1-AS1 and SH3YL1 remains limited. Their priority therefore comes from internal convergence across TWAS, multiple xQTL modalities, and multi-trait colocalization, making them strong candidates for targeted functional annotation. 8.0.9 9. C3orf38: strong statistical triangulation with sparse prior biology For comparative body size at age 10, C3orf38 is a striking EUR result: the gene-level TWAS is highly significant and the same gene–trait pair is supported by both SuSiE-coloc and colocBoost. The colocBoost event is exceptionally compact, with a high-purity confidence set at the locus. Unlike ADCY3 or SLC38A1, C3orf38 has little established placental or growth biology. That contrast is useful. It marks C3orf38 as a novel statistical-triangulation candidate—high priority for follow-up precisely because the genetics are coherent while prior mechanistic expectations are weak. 8.0.10 10. FES illustrates why TWAS and colocalization should not be forced to agree The placental multi-omics literature previously prioritized FES as a likely functional effector at a birth-weight locus [9]. In the current colocBoost output, an EUR FES expression/isoform-expression event colocalizes with the maternal birth-weight GWAS in a one-variant confidence set. Yet FES is not significant in the current gene-level TWAS (acat_q is well above 0.05 for maternal birth weight). This discordance is informative rather than contradictory. TWAS power depends on the predictive weight model and the linear combination of cis variants; colocalization asks whether association patterns share a causal signal. A locus may therefore colocalize convincingly without producing a significant genetically predicted-expression association. FES should be retained as a colocalization-supported placental birth-weight candidate, not discarded because it misses the TWAS threshold. 8.0.11 11. Isoform-aware TWAS is a major added value of this atlas Most published placental TWAS or transcriptome-imputation studies have focused on total gene expression. The present pipeline carries long-read-derived isoform prediction models into FUSION and then combines them at the primary-gene level with ACAT. This has two advantages: it can identify a transcript model with substantially stronger association than the corresponding total-expression model; and it provides a bridge back to the xQTL atlas, where isoform expression, isoform usage, alternative TSS/poly(A), intron retention, editing, and stability are separately mapped. The cost is increased correlation and multiplicity. Isoform hits should therefore be interpreted through gene-level aggregation and, where possible, through colocalization or fine-mapping rather than simply counting every significant transcript as an independent discovery. 8.0.12 12. Practical evidence tiers for manuscript prioritization A useful hierarchy for the results is: Tier 1 — TWAS + colocalization + independent placental biology. Examples include CLDN7/CTDNEP1 at chr17p13 and SLC38A1. These are the strongest candidates for mechanistic discussion. Tier 2 — TWAS + colocalization, limited prior placental literature. PLCE1-AS1, SH3YL1, C3orf38, and FAP fit here. These are high-value novel candidates because multiple genetic analyses converge even though external literature is sparse. Tier 3 — recurrent TWAS with established general growth biology but incomplete placental causal evidence. ADCY3, LEP, and LEPR provide strong biological coherence and can anchor the phenotype interpretation, but tissue-specific mediation remains unresolved. Tier 4 — TWAS alone. These associations remain useful for discovery but need the most caution because shared LD and correlated prediction models can generate TWAS signals without a shared causal molecular/GWAS variant. 8.0.13 13. Limitations First, TWAS is not a causal mediation test. Colocalization, conditional analysis, and experimental perturbation are needed to discriminate causal regulation from LD-mediated association [3]. Second, gene-level ACAT combines p-values but does not estimate a single signed effect. The sign of the strongest component TWAS model should not be reported as the direction of the ACAT association without qualification. Third, ancestry-specific weight coverage is highly unequal across GWAS traits. The present EAS and EUR discovery counts cannot be used as a clean test of ancestry heterogeneity. Fourth, prediction R² is modest for many models. Strong GWAS loci can generate statistically compelling TWAS results even when molecular prediction is imperfect, and weak prediction reduces power for true effects. Fifth, several extreme p-values are stored as numerical zero because of floating-point underflow. Ranking among such values requires the underlying test statistic or higher-precision computation rather than the printed p-value. Finally, placenta is a heterogeneous organ. Bulk molecular prediction can mix trophoblast, stromal, vascular, immune, and other cell-type programs. The atlas’s downstream cell-type annotations should therefore be used when translating a gene-level TWAS into a cellular mechanism. 8.0.14 14. Synthesis The TWAS adds a trait-facing layer to the placental xQTL atlas. It recovers canonical body-weight genetics, identifies placental-growth loci with strong prior support, and extends the atlas into isoform-aware predicted molecular phenotypes. The most defensible biological claims arise where TWAS, xQTL–GWAS colocalization, and prior placental biology converge. Three themes stand out. First, chr17p13 (CLDN7/ELP5/CTDNEP1) remains the clearest birth-weight regulatory hotspot. Second, SLC38A1 links the genetic results to a well-established placental nutrient-transport mechanism. Third, PLCE1-AS1, SH3YL1, FAP, and C3orf38 exemplify the atlas’s discovery potential: they gain priority from cross-method convergence rather than from being expected positive controls. At the same time, FES shows why the report should resist a simple “TWAS-significant = causal” framework. Multi-trait colocalization can provide compelling locus evidence even when a prediction-based test is null. The combined Module 6 outputs are therefore most powerful when interpreted as complementary views of the same genetic architecture. 8.0.15 References Gusev Lab. 9 Cell-type attribution 9.1 Executive summary This report summarizes the deconvolution-based cell-type attribution of significant placental xQTLs. The attribution model tests whether the effect of an ancestry-specific lead cis-xQTL varies with estimated placental cell-type abundance: Y = β0 + βGG + βCC + βG × C(G × C) + *Z**γ + ϵ*, where Y is the normalized molecular phenotype, G is the Module-05 lead cis-xQTL dosage, C is the transformed cell-type proportion, and Z contains the optimized xQTL covariates with the target cell-type covariate removed. The cell-type attribution statistic is βG × C. Primary cell types are assigned only when the best cell-type interaction passes the configured feature-attribution threshold (0.05). The supplied results contain 56,812 genotype × cell-type tests spanning 8,116 significant xQTL features. Using the current aggregate evidence files, 0 unique genes are prioritized by significant TWAS, a positive SuSiE-coloc call, and/or a mixed xQTL–GWAS colocBoost CoS. Across all ancestry-feature combinations, 1,522 features (18.8%) received a significant primary-cell-type assignment. The gene-level integration below is rebuilt directly from the feature-level source table at knit time, so it remains synchronized when coloc/TWAS aggregation changes. ancestry significant_xQTL_features assigned_features assignment_rate modalities EAS 3606 1480 41.0% 9 EUR 4510 42 0.9% 9 Feature-level cell-type attribution summary by ancestry Follow-up diagnostic summary. EUR’s N≈136 is the full analysis cohort, not hidden sample loss. EAS assigns 41.0% of significant xQTL features at full N, and still assigns a median 16.1% after repeated downsampling to N=136, versus 0.9% in EUR. Median residualized G×cell interaction information is 7.1× higher in EAS. Robust HC3 inference further reduces the number of supported assignments, so ancestry differences in attribution yield should not be interpreted as ancestry differences in biology. Interpretation note. An assignment means that the lead xQTL’s estimated genetic effect changes with a deconvolved cell proportion. It is an attribution from bulk-tissue interaction modeling, not direct measurement of an xQTL within purified or single cells. In particular: xqtl_celltype_interactions.tsv.gz should be used for statistical details, sensitivity analyses, and plots of genetic effect as a function of cell composition. xqtl_celltype_annotation.tsv.gz is appropriate for a one-label summary of each significant xQTL feature, but unassigned should be retained rather than forcing every xQTL to a cell type. Gene-level cell-type interpretation should be generated from the current union of downstream evidence rather than assuming gene_celltype_annotation.tsv is synchronized after every aggregation rerun. The report therefore rebuilds the prioritized-gene layer from SuSiE-coloc, mixed xQTL–GWAS colocBoost events, and significant gene-level TWAS, then maps those genes back to the feature-level attribution source table. Cell-type evidence should be ancestry matched. An EAS G×cell assignment is useful biological context for a EUR-only colocBoost or SuSiE-coloc gene, but it should not be described as ancestry-matched support for that EUR event. Likewise, pooled TWAS does not by itself specify an ancestry for the G×cell annotation. The source modality and phenotype should always be retained because different molecular features of the same gene can have different cell-type interactions. The Stage-50 diagnostics show that EUR’s low attribution yield is not caused by hidden sample loss. EAS downsampling to N=136 reduces attribution substantially but still leaves a much higher assignment rate than observed in EUR; EUR also has markedly less residualized G×cell interaction information and weaker minor-allele support across the cell-composition range. The ancestry contrast should therefore be interpreted primarily as a power/information difference, not as evidence that cell-type-specific regulation is biologically rarer in EUR. HC3 robust inference is substantially more conservative than classical OLS in these data, especially for the apparent splicing signals. Classical assignments remain the production output summarized elsewhere in this report, but HC3 results should be treated as an important robustness qualifier. Maternal-contamination sensitivity results provide an important check that an apparent fetal-cell attribution is not primarily driven by variation in maternal contribution to bulk placental tissue. 10 Genotype × pre-pregnancy BMI interactions 10.1 Executive summary This report describes placenta genotype × maternal pre-pregnancy BMI (G×ppBMI) interaction mapping from Module 07 of the Placenta xQTL Atlas. It is a descriptive report of the supplied results, not a re-analysis of individual-level data. The merged Tier-1 results contain 444,582 ancestry-specific feature tests for the exact exposure label ppBMI. At q <= r params$tier1_q, 2,067 rows are significant, representing 2,064 molecular features and approximately 1,449 Ensembl genes. Splicing accounts for 86.2% of significant Tier-1 rows, with a particularly strong contribution from EUR. Cross-ancestry Tier-1 synthesis identifies 1,285 features with ACAT feature-level q <= r params$tier1_q. Only 2 features are significant in both ancestries, and the ancestry-specific lead variants for those features are not the same. Thus, the strongest cross-ancestry conclusion is evidence for recurrent G×ppBMI regulation of the same molecular phenotype, not direct replication of an identical variant-level interaction. Tier 2 contains 35,090 prioritized phenotype-level results, of which 33,949 (96.7%) have q_meta <= r params$tier2_q. Because Tier 2 is a hypothesis-driven follow-up set and many rows are supported by only one ancestry, this near-saturated q-value yield should not be interpreted as 33,949 independent discoveries. A deliberately stricter sensitivity definition requiring two ancestries, concordant interaction direction, nominal P < r params$ancestry_nominal_p in both ancestries, and P_het >= r params$heterogeneity_p retains 664 features. 10.2 Inputs and provenance input_table <- data.table( object = names(paths), path = unname(paths), rows = c(nrow(tier1_all), if (!is.na(paths["tier1_significant"])) nrow(read_tab(paths["tier1_significant"])) else NA_integer_, nrow(tier1_meta_all), nrow(tier2_all), nrow(summary_all), nrow(status_all)) ) kable(input_table, caption = "G×E aggregate inputs used by this report.") object path rows tier1_results /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/gxe/gxe_tier1_results.tsv.gz 889164 tier1_significant /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/gxe/gxe_tier1_significant.tsv 2067 tier1_meta /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/gxe/gxe_tier1_meta.tsv.gz 273602 tier2_results /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/gxe/gxe_tier2_results.tsv.gz 35090 summary /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/gxe/gxe_summary.tsv 414 run_status /Users/stbresnahan/Documents/GitHub/Placenta_xQTL_atlas/reports/gxe/gxe_run_status.tsv 434 G×E aggregate inputs used by this report. Module 07 README: Tier-1 scan: Tier-1 cross-ancestry synthesis: Tier-2 prioritized scan: 10.3 Analysis framework For each molecular phenotype, Module 07 fits a cis interaction model of the form Y = βGG + βEE + βG × E(G × E) + *Z**γ + ϵ*, where E is standardized ppBMI, G is genotype dosage, and Z contains the optimized molecular-QTL covariates. The parameter of interest is βG × E: the change in the genotype effect per one-SD increase in ppBMI. Tier 1 is ancestry-specific discovery with adaptive phenotype-level permutation and FDR control within ancestry × modality × exposure. Cross-ancestry synthesis is performed after ancestry-specific discovery. When ancestry lead variants differ, the repository deliberately labels the feature as discordant-lead and does not claim that the IVW statistic represents the same variant-level test. Tier 2 is a hypothesis-driven scan of phenotypes prioritized from downstream genetic evidence (colocalization and significant isoTWAS/gene-level TWAS criteria in the current implementation). It performs nominal cis interaction testing within each ancestry, then variant-level IVW meta-analysis where possible, retains the best meta-analysis variant for each prioritized phenotype, and applies BH correction across the prioritized set. 10.4 Pipeline completion status_display <- copy(run_status) status_display <- status_display[order(factor(component, c("tier1","tier1_meta","tier2")), The reported coefficient asks whether the genotype–molecular-phenotype relationship changes across ppBMI. Ancestry-specific lead variants are not interchangeable. A phenotype significant in EAS and EUR can still have different lead variants, so opposite signs at discordant leads do not establish effect reversal of the same allele. Tier 1 and Tier 2 answer different questions. Tier 1 is discovery; Tier 2 is genetically prioritized follow-up and is therefore enriched by construction. The Tier-2 q-value distribution is unusually saturated. Two-ancestry concordance, nominal ancestry-level evidence, and heterogeneity are useful reporting diagnostics. Modality counts are correlated. Multiple splice junctions, isoforms, or 3’/5’ events from the same gene are not independent biological discoveries. Effect magnitudes are scale-dependent. ppBMI and molecular phenotypes are standardized according to the Module-07 workflow, so coefficients should be interpreted in that standardized context. No causal claim follows from G×E alone. These results identify ppBMI-dependent genetic regulation; causal mediation of pregnancy outcomes requires additional evidence. 10.10 Reusable output tables generated <- list.files(params$tables_dir, full.names = TRUE) kable(data.table(file = basename(generated)), caption = "Tables written by this report.") file gxe_internal_evidence_gene_summary.tsv tier1_cross_ancestry_summary.tsv tier1_recurrent_genes.tsv tier1_significant_both_ancestries.tsv tier1_top_signals.tsv tier1_yield_by_ancestry_modality.tsv tier2_robust_recurrent_genes.tsv tier2_robust_top_signals.tsv tier2_yield_by_modality.tsv Tables written by this report. 10.11 Conclusions The ppBMI G×E atlas provides strong evidence that placental cis-regulatory effects can vary across the maternal pre-pregnancy BMI spectrum. The principal descriptive features are: a large Tier-1 interaction set with pronounced ancestry and modality heterogeneity; a dominant splicing contribution, especially in EUR; very limited direct feature-level significance in both ancestries and widespread discordance of ancestry-specific lead variants; a large, enriched Tier-2 follow-up set whose near-saturated q-value yield warrants stricter two-ancestry sensitivity summaries; and a smaller subset of recurrent genes and molecular phenotypes supported by multiple internal G×ppBMI evidence dimensions. The most defensible next prioritization step is to combine these G×ppBMI signals with the independent fine-mapping, colocalization/colocBoost, TWAS, and cell-type attribution evidence generated elsewhere in the Placenta xQTL Atlas.
