11 Literature context: G×ppBMI findings

11 Literature context: G×ppBMI findings Placenta xQTL Atlas — Module 07 G×E (ppBMI) Review date: 2026-10-12 11.0.1 Scope This review places the current placenta genotype × maternal pre-pregnancy BMI (G×ppBMI) results in the context of prior work on maternal adiposity, placental molecular biology, and BMI-dependent genetic regulation. The project results are treated as the primary evidence; external literature is used to assess biological plausibility and novelty. A critical distinction is maintained throughout: most prior placental studies test maternal BMI or obesity main effects on placental molecular traits, whereas the present analysis asks whether genetic effects on placental molecular phenotypes vary as a function of ppBMI. A BMI-associated placental gene is therefore not automatically a G×BMI gene, and vice versa. 11.0.2 Summary of the current ppBMI G×E results The supplied Module-07 aggregates contain 444,582 ancestry-specific Tier-1 feature tests for the exact ppBMI exposure label. At q < 0.05, there are 2,067 significant ancestry-specific rows representing 2,064 unique molecular features. Splicing accounts for 1,782 of these rows (86.2%), with a particularly large EUR contribution. Cross-ancestry synthesis is much more restrictive. Only two molecular features are significant in both EAS and EUR, and neither uses the same ancestry-specific lead variant. The features map to TAF6 and MRAS. These should be described as recurrent cross-ancestry molecular phenotypes rather than variant-level replications. Across the broader Tier-1 meta table, 1,285 features pass the feature-level ACAT q-value threshold. Tier 2 contains 35,090 genetically prioritized phenotypes. Although 33,949 (96.7%) have q_meta < 0.05, most are supported by only one ancestry and the set was pre-enriched by external genetic prioritization. Requiring two ancestries, concordant interaction direction, nominal P < 0.05 in both ancestries, and P_heterogeneity >= 0.05 reduces the set to 664 molecular features. That stricter subset is more useful for biological prioritization than the raw Tier-2 q-value count. 11.0.3 1. Maternal adiposity measurably alters placental molecular state There is strong prior evidence that maternal BMI and obesity affect the human placental transcriptome, epigenome, and metabolic environment. A 2024 genome-wide RNA-seq study of 450 placentas from the Gen3G cohort found that higher maternal BMI in early pregnancy was associated with lower placental EPYC expression and higher IGFBP6, CHRDL1, and CXCL13 expression after multiple-testing correction [1]. This establishes that maternal BMI can be reflected in the term placental transcriptome even after adjustment for major pregnancy covariates. Earlier placental transcriptome studies reached broadly consistent pathway-level conclusions. In a small case-control study, maternal pre-pregnancy obesity was associated with 72 differentially regulated placental genes and with inflammation/immune, lipid-metabolism, cancer, and angiogenesis pathways [2]. A separate RNA-seq study of placentas from lean versus obese pregnancies found 288 differentially expressed genes and evidence for altered lipid metabolism, angiogenesis, hormone activity, cytokine activity, oxidative stress, and lipotoxicity [3]. These studies are not G×E analyses, but they support ppBMI as a biologically meaningful placental environment. Placental epigenetic studies provide a parallel line of evidence. In the NICHD Fetal Growth Studies, pre-pregnancy BMI was associated with placental DNA methylation at loci including EGFL7 and VEZT; both ppBMI and methylation at the EGFL7-associated CpG were negatively correlated with placental EGFL7 expression [4]. Thus maternal adiposity is capable of engaging multiple molecular layers of the placenta. 11.0.3.1 Implication for the present atlas The present G×ppBMI results extend this literature from mean molecular differences by BMI to genotype-dependent molecular responses across BMI. They are therefore conceptually complementary rather than redundant. 11.0.4 2. BMI-dependent regulatory effects are biologically established Human G×BMI regulatory mapping has precedent outside placenta. Glastonbury and colleagues analyzed RNA-seq from 856 female twins across multiple tissues and identified cis G×BMI effects on gene expression, with significant interactions concentrated in adipose tissue and enriched in adipocyte enhancers and metabolic/inflammatory programs [5]. This study is important for two reasons: it shows that BMI can act as a continuous regulatory environment, and it demonstrates that G×BMI effects can be strongly tissue-specific. More recently, Signer and colleagues used an interaction framework to map BMI-dynamic eQTLs across tissues and showed that BMI-by-genotype models can identify context-dependent regulatory relationships influenced by cell type, putative enhancer activity, and inflammatory cytokines [6]. Their results further support the general premise that a SNP’s regulatory effect is not necessarily fixed across an individual’s physiological environment. 11.0.4.1 Relevance to placenta Neither study establishes the specific placental interactions observed here. Instead, they validate the regulatory model class: BMI is a plausible continuous context that can modify genetic control of gene expression. The placenta is especially appropriate for this question because it is directly exposed to the maternal metabolic milieu while retaining a fetal genotype. 11.0.5 3. The strong splicing signal has emerging biological precedent The most striking feature of the ppBMI Tier-1 results is the predominance of splicing interactions. This pattern should be treated as a major hypothesis, not as already-established biology, because direct human placental genotype×ppBMI splicing studies remain sparse. Two recent studies nevertheless make the observation biologically plausible. First, a 2026 rat time-series placental RNA-seq study reported that maternal high-fat diet disrupted placental spliceosome pathways during mid-to-late gestation, including altered expression of multiple spliceosome genes [7]. Importantly, the authors observed spliceosome disruption even in obesity-resistant animals, suggesting that metabolic/dietary context and adiposity phenotype need not be interchangeable. Second, a 2026 human study found widespread differential pre-mRNA splicing in placentas from pregnancies affected by gestational diabetes mellitus and implicated SRSF10 as a regulator of a subset of the missplicing [8]. Gestational diabetes is not ppBMI, and this study did not test genotype interactions, but it independently demonstrates that placental RNA processing is responsive to a metabolic pregnancy environment. 11.0.5.1 Interpretation The atlas result therefore fits an emerging model in which placental splicing is metabolically responsive. The novel contribution is the suggestion that the magnitude of cis-genetic control over splicing itself depends on maternal ppBMI. Replication in an independent placenta cohort would be particularly valuable because the number and correlation structure of splice events can magnify modality-level counts. 11.0.6 4. Tier-1 candidate loci 11.0.6.1 CFLAR CFLAR is among the strongest/recurrent Tier-1 signals, with significant ppBMI interactions across molecular modalities and ancestries. The strongest current signal is an EAS alternative-polyadenylation phenotype. CFLAR encodes FLICE-inhibitory protein (FLIP), an inhibitor of caspase-8. Human placental work has demonstrated long and short FLIP isoforms in early and late gestation placenta and in trophoblast cells, with expression patterns varying by cell lineage and differentiation state [9]. The study interpreted FLIP as an important component of trophoblast survival. This provides direct placental biological support for CFLAR, although not for a maternal-BMI interaction specifically. A ppBMI-dependent regulatory effect at CFLAR is mechanistically plausible in a placenta exposed to obesity-related inflammatory and oxidative-stress pathways, but functional validation is needed. Evidence assessment: strong placental relevance; G×ppBMI mechanism novel. 11.0.6.2 PRLR PRLR has multiple significant Tier-1 splicing features, particularly in EUR. The prolactin receptor is directly expressed in human fetal membranes, decidua, placenta, and trophoblast compartments [10]. The broader placental lactogenic axis is also sensitive to maternal obesity: obesity has been associated with disrupted placental lactogen chromosomal architecture and more than a 40% decrease in term human placental lactogen RNA in one study [11]. These observations make PRLR one of the more compelling biologically contextualized G×ppBMI candidates. They do not establish that PRLR splicing is caused by obesity or that the current interacting variant is functional. Evidence assessment: direct placental receptor evidence plus obesity- sensitive lactogenic context; specific G×ppBMI splicing effect novel. 11.0.6.3 SKP2 SKP2 shows significant G×ppBMI evidence across more than one molecular phenotype in the results. A 2026 placental study showed that SKP2 is highly expressed in placenta and co-expressed in syncytiotrophoblast precursor, syncytiotrophoblast, and cytotrophoblast populations; it also identified a RhoBTB1/CUL3-dependent mechanism regulating SKP2 stability [12]. This is unusually direct recent placental evidence for a project hit. The connection to maternal BMI remains untested experimentally. Evidence assessment: strong contemporary placental evidence; ppBMI- dependent genetic regulation novel. 11.0.6.4 SGMS1 SGMS1, encoding sphingomyelin synthase 1, has recurrent EUR splicing signals in the current Tier-1 results. Maternal obesity is well established to alter placental lipid metabolism and create a lipotoxic/oxidative-stress environment [3]. This gives SGMS1 a coherent pathway-level rationale, but the literature reviewed here does not provide direct evidence that SGMS1 itself is a placental maternal-BMI target. Evidence assessment: strong pathway plausibility; direct locus-level placental G×ppBMI evidence currently limited. 11.0.6.5 SLC25A36 SLC25A36, a mitochondrial carrier, is another recurrent Tier-1 signal. Maternal obesity has been linked to altered placental lipid handling, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial biology [3]. As with SGMS1, this supports the biological neighborhood rather than the specific gene–variant interaction. Evidence assessment: mitochondrial/metabolic plausibility; direct placental G×ppBMI evidence limited. 11.0.6.6 SYT8 SYT8 is one of the most recurrent Tier-1 genes by number of significant features and appears across ancestry-specific results. Outside placenta, SYT8 has been linked to glucose-regulated insulin-secretory biology, making it a plausible metabolic-context candidate. However, the literature reviewed for this report did not identify strong direct evidence connecting SYT8 to maternal obesity in human placenta. Evidence assessment: interesting metabolic candidate; placental G×ppBMI role appears novel. 11.0.6.7 PBRM1 PBRM1 appears across significant molecular features and ancestries in the project. PBRM1 is a chromatin-remodeling component with reproductive biology evidence, but direct human placental maternal-BMI evidence is currently thin. Its value here is therefore primarily statistical/internal until validated. Evidence assessment: mechanistically plausible chromatin regulator; placental ppBMI specificity novel. 11.0.6.8 TAF6 and MRAS: cross-ancestry molecular recurrence The only two Tier-1 molecular features significant in both EAS and EUR map to TAF6 and MRAS. This is important evidence of cross-ancestry recurrence at the phenotype level, but it is not same-variant replication: both features have different ancestry-specific lead variants. MRAS also has different interaction directions at the two distinct leads. These loci should therefore be prioritized for locus-level conditional or joint fine-mapping rather than described as replicated allele-specific G×ppBMI effects. 11.0.7 5. Tier-2 candidates and how to use them Tier 2 is enriched by design because it begins with loci supported by colocalization and/or TWAS-based criteria. Its very high rate of q_meta < 0.05 therefore cannot be compared directly with Tier-1 discovery yield. A stricter two-ancestry sensitivity subset retains 664 features. Recurrent genes in this set include CCDC107, ACTG1, CUTA, CNGA1, DAXX, BTN3A2, CLEC1A, and RPS18, among others. These are useful targets for integrated prioritization, especially when the same gene also has independent fine-mapping, colocalization/colocBoost, TWAS, or cell-type evidence. The literature review should not assign equal biological weight to every Tier-2 q-value. In particular: one-ancestry Tier-2 rows are discovery/follow-up evidence, not replication; the selected variant is the best meta-analysis variant within a pre-prioritized phenotype; molecular phenotypes from the same gene are correlated; and for one-ancestry rows, the final normal-theory meta z-test can be more extreme than the finite-df ancestry nominal p-value. The two-ancestry, directionally concordant subset is therefore the preferable Tier-2 layer for headline biological interpretation. 11.0.8 6. Ancestry heterogeneity is a result, not merely a nuisance The project shows major ancestry differences in the number and distribution of G×ppBMI discoveries. This can arise from several nonexclusive sources: sample-size/power differences, allele-frequency differences, genotype support within the exposure distribution, LD structure, distinct ancestry-specific lead variants, and true biological heterogeneity. The current data do not justify concluding that ppBMI-dependent regulation is intrinsically more prevalent in one ancestry. The scarcity of same-lead cross-ancestry features makes that especially important. Ancestry-specific results should remain primary, with cross-ancestry summaries serving as a synthesis layer. 11.0.9 7. Integrated biological interpretation Taken together, the results and prior literature support four working hypotheses. Maternal adiposity is a genuine placental molecular environment. Human transcriptomic and epigenetic studies consistently demonstrate placental responses to maternal BMI and obesity [1-4]. Genetic regulation can be BMI-dependent. Human G×BMI eQTL studies show that adiposity modifies regulatory variant effects in a strongly tissue/context-specific manner [5,6]. RNA processing may be an important placental metabolic-response layer. The splicing predominance in this atlas is novel, but recent placental metabolic-stress studies independently implicate spliceosome and pre-mRNA-splicing regulation [7,8]. The strongest candidates are those with orthogonal evidence. Genes such as CFLAR, PRLR, and SKP2 combine strong internal interaction evidence with direct placental biology, whereas several other high-ranking loci remain attractive precisely because their placental G×ppBMI roles appear novel. 11.0.10 8. Recommended next analyses For atlas-level prioritization, the most informative next step is to intersect the G×ppBMI results with independent evidence rather than rank on G×E q-value alone. In particular: annotate Tier-1 and robust Tier-2 features with Module-05 credible sets; intersect G×ppBMI genes with SuSiE-coloc and colocBoost loci; overlay TWAS gene-level evidence; use the cell-type interaction annotations to ask whether G×ppBMI loci are concentrated in specific placental cellular contexts; distinguish exact-variant overlap from gene-only overlap; perform locus plots for TAF6 and MRAS to understand the discordant ancestry-specific leads; and where individual-level data permit, pursue joint main+interaction fine-mapping rather than treating the top marginal interaction variant as the causal variant. 11.0.11 Conclusions The placenta ppBMI G×E atlas is consistent with a broader literature in which maternal adiposity reshapes placental molecular state and BMI modifies genetic regulatory effects in human tissues. Its most distinctive observation is the large burden of ppBMI-dependent splicing regulation. The literature provides emerging metabolic-splicing precedent but not direct replication, making this a potentially important novel contribution. The strongest locus-level biological candidates should be prioritized on multiple lines of evidence rather than interaction significance alone. CFLAR, PRLR, and SKP2 have particularly clear independent placental support; TAF6 and MRAS merit focused cross-ancestry locus analysis; and recurrent splicing candidates such as SGMS1, SLC25A36, SYT8, ASPRV1, and others provide a broader discovery set for functional follow-up. 11.0.12 References Sordillo JE, et al. Higher Maternal Body Mass Index Is Associated With Lower Placental Expression of EPYC: A Genome-Wide Transcriptomic Study. 12 Integrated locus prioritization 12.1 Executive summary This report integrates six analytical layers from the Placenta xQTL Atlas: baseline cis-xQTL discovery, SuSHiE fine-mapping, xQTL–GWAS colocalization (pairwise SuSiE-coloc and multi-trait colocBoost), TWAS, genotype × placental-cell-proportion attribution, and genotype × maternal pre-pregnancy BMI (G×ppBMI) interaction mapping. The ranking is deliberately convergence-first. A gene receives one core evidence dimension for each of: high-confidence fine-mapping, GWAS shared-signal evidence, significant TWAS, and Tier-1 G×ppBMI discovery. SuSiE-coloc and colocBoost are combined into one shared-signal dimension because they interrogate the same underlying xQTL/GWAS relationship; agreement between both methods is treated as a strength bonus. Cell-type attribution and baseline xQTL recurrence provide biological context. Robust G×E Tier 2 is also a strength bonus rather than an independent line of evidence because Tier 2 was genetically preselected. Current integrated yield. 3,325 genes have at least one core evidence dimension; 575 genes have ≥2 core dimensions, and 233 meet the report’s Tier-A convergence rule. 365 multi-line genes also carry independent Tier-1 G×ppBMI evidence. Across TWAS and colocalization, 44 gene × GWAS-trait pairs are supported by at least two methods. Approximate coordinate clustering yields 410 loci with ≥2 core evidence dimensions. The highest-ranked multi-line genes in the current run are: YPEL3, MRPL18, SLC38A1, CRAT, SH3YL1, ELP5, PLCE1-AS1, SEMA3F. The leading approximate locus clusters include chr10:91.73–97.72 Mb, chr17:4.6–8.29 Mb, chr6:24.44–27.2 Mb, chr16:30.1–30.77 Mb, chr6:158.27–160.08 Mb. Interpretation priorities The integrated ranking is intended to support manuscript and experimental prioritization. The strongest candidates are those satisfying several of the following simultaneously: a high-confidence fine-mapped placental regulatory signal; evidence that the placental xQTL shares a GWAS signal, ideally supported by both pairwise SuSiE-coloc and colocBoost or by same-lead evidence; a significant TWAS association for the same gene and same GWAS trait; independent Tier-1 G×ppBMI evidence, especially if recurrent across modalities or ancestries; and interpretable cell-type localization. A compact multi-gene region should generally be discussed as a regulatory locus when different methods nominate neighboring genes. The locus-level table above is specifically intended to expose those cases rather than forcing all evidence onto a single gene. 12.10 9. Guardrails and limitations No double counting of coloc methods as separate core lines. SuSiE-coloc and colocBoost use overlapping xQTL/GWAS information. Their concordance increases confidence but does not create two independent biological observations. Tier-2 G×E is selection-enriched. It is not counted as an independent line because it starts from genetically prioritized loci. Tier-1 G×E is the independent interaction-discovery layer. TWAS is not mediation. A significant TWAS association means that a genetically predicted placental molecular phenotype associates with the GWAS trait; it does not by itself establish a causal mediating gene. Fine-mapping is locus resolution, not trait causality. High PIP strengthens variant-level localization of the xQTL but does not imply that the same variant causes the external GWAS trait unless supported by colocalization. Cell-type assignments are contextual. A significant genotype × cell-proportion interaction can localize heterogeneity but does not prove a unique causal placental cell population. The locus clustering is approximate. The locus_gap_bp rule uses observed lead-evidence coordinates and genomic distance, not ancestry-specific LD. Dense hotspots should receive dedicated locus plots and conditional analyses. Gene-level overlap can be weaker than exact feature/variant overlap. For top candidates, the next step should compare the exact fine-mapped credible-set variants, xQTL leads, G×E leads, and GWAS credible signals. 12.11 10.
